title: Reading the night sky: why the stars turn, how the Pole Star shows where you are, and how astronomers measure how far away a star is

summary.text: Watch the night sky for an hour and every star slides slowly across it, except one that hardly moves. That star is the Pole Star, called Dhruva in India, and it is how travellers have found north for thousands of years. It stands about 13 degrees above the northern horizon in Chennai, but about 29 degrees in Delhi, so its height tells you how far north you are. Your child works out why with a ball and a straw, measures how far the sky turns in one hour, and uses a thumb and a wall to measure distances the way astronomers measure the distance to stars. Along the way: why Orion is a winter star and Scorpius a summer one, why a red star is cooler than a blue one, and why planets do not twinkle but stars do.
summary.art: A child on a terrace at night with a straw taped to a protractor, aiming at a faint star above the northern rooftops, with a long exposure of circling star trails drawn in the sky above.

intro.hook: On a clear night, look north and find the Saptarishi, the seven stars shaped like a ladle. Two of them, Kratu and Pulaha, point at a lonely star called Dhruva, the Pole Star. Watch for an hour, and all the other stars swing slowly round it, like the spokes of a wheel round the hub. What is the sky turning around, and why does that one star stay still?
intro.text: In this unit you find out. You build a model with a ball and a straw that shows why the Pole Star stands higher in the sky the further north you go. You measure with your fist how far the stars move in an hour. You use the jump of your thumb to measure distances, which is how astronomers first measured the distance to a star. You also learn why Orion and Scorpius never share a night sky, how a star's colour shows its temperature, and how sailors crossed oceans with nothing but the stars.
intro.art: A hand-drawn night sky with the seven stars of the Saptarishi, a dotted line from the two pointer stars to a lone star in the middle, and curved arrows showing other stars circling around it.

outcomes: I can explain that the stars seem to turn once a day because the Earth spins, and that the sky turns about 15 degrees every hour.
I can find the Pole Star from the two pointer stars of the Saptarishi, and say why it stays almost still while other stars circle it.
I can explain why the height of the Pole Star above the horizon equals my latitude, and why some stars never set where I live.
I can explain why different stars are up at night in different seasons, using the Earth's journey round the Sun.
I can explain how parallax measures distance, and use the jump of my thumb to find how far away something is.
I can tell the difference between how bright a star looks and how bright it really is, and say what a star's colour shows about its temperature.
I can tell a planet from a star in the night sky, and explain why stars twinkle and planets mostly do not.

terms.meaning: The point in the sky straight above the Earth's North Pole, where the Earth's axis points. The whole sky seems to turn round this point.
terms.example: The north celestial pole is very close to the Pole Star.
terms.art: The Earth with its axis drawn as a long line pointing up into the sky towards a star, and circles of stars round that point.

terms.meaning: The bright star closest to the north celestial pole. In English it is called Polaris. In Sanskrit it is Dhruva, which means fixed or firm. It seems to stay still while all other stars circle it.
terms.example: You can find the Pole Star by following a line from Pulaha through Kratu, the two pointer stars of the Saptarishi.
terms.art: The seven stars of the Saptarishi with a dotted line through the two end stars of the bowl pointing to a single star.

terms.meaning: The horizon is the line where the sky seems to meet the ground. A star's altitude is how high it is above the horizon, measured in degrees. The horizon is 0 degrees, and straight overhead is 90.
terms.example: A fist held out at arm's length covers about 10 degrees of sky, so a star two fists up has an altitude of about 20 degrees.
terms.art: A child holding out a fist at arm's length, with a star stacked two fists above the horizon and a scale from 0 to 90 degrees drawn up the sky.

terms.meaning: How far north or south of the equator a place is, measured in degrees. The equator is 0 degrees and the North Pole is 90 degrees north.
terms.example: Kanyakumari is at about 8 degrees north, Chennai about 13, Hyderabad about 17, Mumbai about 19, and Delhi about 29.
terms.art: A globe with lines of latitude drawn across it, and India with dots for Kanyakumari, Chennai, Mumbai and Delhi on their lines.

terms.meaning: A star that goes round the Pole Star in a circle that stays above the horizon, so it never sets. Which stars are circumpolar depends on your latitude.
terms.example: From Delhi, the stars close to the Pole Star never set. From the equator, no star is circumpolar.
terms.art: A circle of star trails round the Pole Star, all above the horizon line, and another star's trail dipping below the horizon.

terms.meaning: The path the Sun seems to follow through the stars during a year. The Moon and the planets stay close to this path too. The constellations along it are the zodiac.
terms.example: In January the Sun lies in front of the stars of Sagittarius, so those stars are hidden by daylight.
terms.art: A great circle drawn across the sky with twelve constellation pictures along it and the Sun at one point on it.

terms.meaning: The apparent shift of a near thing against a far background when you look from two different places. Your thumb seems to jump when you close one eye and open the other. The nearer the thing, the bigger the jump.
terms.example: Astronomers measure the parallax of a star by looking at it six months apart, from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit.
terms.art: A thumb held in front of a face, seen first by the left eye and then by the right against a far wall, with two small marks where it seems to be.

terms.meaning: The distance between the two places you look from when you measure parallax. A longer baseline gives a bigger shift, which is easier to measure.
terms.example: For your thumb, the baseline is the gap between your eyes, about 6 centimetres. For a star, it is the width of the Earth's orbit, about 300 million kilometres.
terms.art: A long line between two dots labelled eye and eye for a thumb, and a much longer line across the Earth's orbit for a star.

terms.meaning: Finding the distance to something by drawing a triangle. You measure a baseline and the angle to the thing from each end. The shape of the triangle then gives the distance.
terms.example: Surveyors triangulated across India in the 1800s to map the country. They started near Chennai with a baseline of several kilometres.
terms.art: A triangle drawn on the ground with two people at the ends of a base line and a tall tree at the point, with angles marked at each person.

terms.meaning: How bright a star looks from here. It depends on how much light the star gives out and also on how far away it is.
terms.example: The Sun looks by far the brightest star because it is so close. Canopus looks bright, but it is far away and truly very powerful.
terms.art: Two lamps, one small and near and one huge and far away, that look equally bright to a child standing between them.

terms.meaning: How much light a star really gives out, whatever its distance. Astronomers call this luminosity and compare it with the Sun's.
terms.example: Sirius gives out about 25 times as much light as the Sun. Rigel gives out tens of thousands of times as much.
terms.art: A row of stars of different sizes, each with a number below showing how many Suns of light it gives out.

terms.meaning: A number for how bright a star looks. A smaller number means a brighter star. About 130 years before the Common Era, the Greek astronomer Hipparchus put stars into six classes, from 1 for the brightest to 6 for the faintest.
terms.example: The Pole Star has a magnitude of about 2. The faintest stars you can see in a dark place are about 6.
terms.art: A scale from 1 to 6 with bright and faint stars along it, and a downward arrow from bright to faint.

terms.meaning: The colour of a star shows how hot its surface is. Cooler stars look red or orange, medium stars look yellow, and the hottest stars look blue-white.
terms.example: Antares, called Jyeshtha, is red and about 3,500 degrees Celsius. The Sun is yellow-white and about 5,500. Sirius is blue-white and about 10,000.
terms.art: Four stars in a row coloured red, yellow, white and blue-white, with temperatures below them rising from left to right.

terms.meaning: The quick flicker in the brightness and colour of a star. It is made by the Earth's moving air, not by the star. Planets look like tiny discs and twinkle much less.
terms.example: A star near the horizon twinkles more than a star overhead, because its light crosses more air.
terms.art: A beam of starlight passing through wavy layers of air before reaching a child's eye, with the star shown flickering in several colours.

terms.meaning: The word planet comes from a Greek word for wanderer. From the Earth, the planets seem to wander through the star patterns over days and months, while the stars keep their places.
terms.example: Jupiter takes about a year to move across one constellation of the zodiac.
terms.art: A bright planet drawn at four dates as it moves slowly across a fixed pattern of stars.

terms.meaning: The slow wobble of the Earth's axis, like the wobble of a spinning top. It makes the north celestial pole trace a circle in the sky once in about 26,000 years.
terms.example: About 4,700 years ago, a star called Thuban was nearest the north pole. In about 12,000 years it will be Vega.
terms.art: A spinning top tilted and wobbling, with its axis drawing a circle against a background of stars.

explanations.concept: Why the whole sky seems to turn once a day
explanations.definition: The Earth spins once on its axis about every 24 hours. So the stars seem to circle us, the way scenery seems to move past the window of a train. The sky turns about 15 degrees every hour.
explanations.description: If you take a photo of the night sky with a long exposure, each star leaves a curved trail. The trails are parts of circles with the Pole Star near the middle. In an hour, each star has moved through an arc of about 15 degrees, which is one-twenty-fourth of a full circle. The Sun and the Moon rise in the east and set in the west for the same reason. It is the Earth that turns, towards the east, and not the sky that turns towards the west. In 1851, in Paris, Leon Foucault hung a heavy ball on a very long wire and let it swing. Its line of swing slowly turned all through the day, which showed that the floor beneath it was turning. Many science museums have a Foucault pendulum.
examples: A long photo of the sky shows the stars as arcs. In a one-hour photo, every arc covers the same angle, about 15 degrees.
A star that rises due east at 8 pm will be at its highest point, halfway across the sky, by 2 am, six hours later.
Looking north, the stars circle the Pole Star anticlockwise. Looking south, they move across the sky from the left to the right.
explanations.art: A long-exposure photograph of the night sky with concentric star trails round a bright centre, and a note that each arc is 15 degrees per hour.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea behind the turning sky: it is the Earth that turns.

explanations.concept: The Pole Star and the point the sky turns round
explanations.definition: The Earth's axis points almost exactly at the Pole Star. Because the axis points there, the Pole Star does not seem to move as the Earth spins, and all the other stars circle it.
explanations.description: Think of a spinning top. The point at the end of its axis stays still while everything else goes round. The Earth's axis points to a spot in the sky called the north celestial pole, and the Pole Star lies within a degree of it. That is why it is the one star that hardly moves. It is not a bright star, but it is easy to find from the Saptarishi. Take the two stars at the outer edge of the bowl, Pulaha (at the bottom) and Kratu (at the rim). Draw a line from Pulaha through Kratu and carry on, about five times the gap between them. The line ends at the Pole Star. In the stories of India, Dhruva was a boy who was given a place in the sky that would never move. There is no bright star near the south celestial pole.
examples: The Pole Star is about as bright as the stars of the Saptarishi. It is not the brightest star in the sky, as many people think.
Another way to find it is from Cassiopeia, a W-shaped group of stars on the other side of the Pole Star from the Saptarishi.
Sailors and travellers found north by the Pole Star for thousands of years, long before the magnetic compass.
explanations.art: The Saptarishi with a line through its two pointer stars, a measuring hand showing five gaps, and the Pole Star at the end with a stick marking the north horizon.
explanations.context: This card explains what the Pole Star is and how to find it.

explanations.concept: The height of the Pole Star equals your latitude
explanations.definition: The altitude of the Pole Star above your northern horizon, in degrees, is about the same as your latitude. It is 0 degrees at the equator and 90 degrees at the North Pole.
explanations.description: The Pole Star is so far away that its light comes to every part of the Earth along the same direction. So the direction to the Pole Star is parallel to the Earth's axis wherever you stand. Imagine standing at the North Pole. The axis points straight up, so the Pole Star is overhead, at 90 degrees. On the equator, the axis lies flat along the ground, so the Pole Star sits on the northern horizon, at 0 degrees. In between, the star's height grows steadily with how far north you are. This is why a traveller walking north sees the Pole Star climb. A wanderer can find their latitude without a map. Polaris is not exactly on the pole, so the rule is right to within about one degree.
examples: In Kanyakumari, at 8 degrees north, the Pole Star is less than one fist above the northern horizon and is often hidden by haze.
In Chennai it is at about 13 degrees, which is one fist and a bit.
In Delhi it is at about 29 degrees, nearly three fists high.
explanations.art: A globe with a long line along its axis towards the Pole Star, and small observers at the pole, the equator and Chennai, each with a flat horizon card and a pointing straw.
explanations.context: This card explains why the Pole Star stands higher the further north you go. The ball-and-straw model shows the same idea.

explanations.concept: Stars that never set, and stars you never see
explanations.definition: A star is circumpolar if its circle round the Pole Star stays above your horizon. All stars within your latitude's number of degrees of the Pole Star are circumpolar for you. Stars close enough to the south pole never rise for you.
explanations.description: The Pole Star stands at your latitude in degrees above the horizon. A star that circles the Pole Star at a distance smaller than that never dips below the horizon. In Delhi at 29 degrees, stars within 29 degrees of the Pole Star never set. In Chennai at 13 degrees, only stars within 13 degrees never set. On the equator, nothing is circumpolar, and every star rises and sets. The same rule works in the south. In Chennai, stars within 13 degrees of the south pole never rise. So the stars you can see depend on where you live. From the southern tip of India, the Southern Cross can be seen low in the south on spring evenings, but it can never be seen from Kashmir.
examples: From Kashmir, at about 34 degrees north, Kratu, the star at the corner of the Saptarishi's bowl, never sets.
From Chennai, the Saptarishi rides high on spring evenings and sinks to the northern horizon, or below it, on autumn evenings.
A traveller going from Delhi to Kanyakumari sees new stars appear low in the south that were never visible at home.
explanations.art: A circle on a star map round the Pole Star, its size equal to the observer's latitude, with stars inside labelled never sets and stars far outside labelled sets.
explanations.context: This card explains why some stars are up all night and others are never seen from where you live.

explanations.concept: Why the evening sky changes with the seasons
explanations.definition: The Earth goes round the Sun once a year. At night we face away from the Sun, so each month we look out towards a different part of space. Stars rise about 2 hours earlier each month.
explanations.description: Each day, a star rises about 4 minutes earlier than the day before. In a month that adds up to about 2 hours. So after a few months, a star that rose at sunset has moved to rise in the afternoon, and then it can be seen only in the morning. After six months, it is up during the day and hidden by the Sun's glare. After a year, it is back where it began. The constellations opposite the Sun are up at midnight. In January, the Sun lies in front of Sagittarius, and Gemini is at its highest at midnight. The Sun's yearly path through the stars is the ecliptic, and the constellations along it are the zodiac. The Moon and the planets stay near this path.
examples: Orion, with its three belt stars and the red star Ardra, is a winter evening group in India. It is high at midnight in December.
Scorpius, with the red star Jyeshtha, is highest at midnight around June and is a summer evening group.
The full Moon is always opposite the Sun, so it sits in the group of stars that is highest at midnight that month.
explanations.art: The Sun at the middle, the Earth at four points on its orbit, and for each point an arrow showing which group of stars is straight behind the Earth at midnight.
explanations.context: This card explains why different stars are up in different months. The lamp-and-cards activity shows the same idea.

explanations.concept: Parallax: measuring distance with two viewpoints
explanations.definition: Parallax is the shift in position of a near thing against a far background when you look from two places. The nearer the thing, the larger the shift. If you know the baseline and measure the shift, you can find the distance.
explanations.description: Hold a pencil at arm's length and close one eye, then the other. The pencil seems to jump against the wall. Now hold it closer to your nose and the jump is bigger. If you measure the jump, you can work out how far away the pencil is. Astronomers do the same with stars, but they need a baseline much wider than the gap between eyes. They look at a star in January and again in July, when the Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit, 300 million kilometres away. A near star shifts a tiny bit against the far stars behind it. The Gaia spacecraft has measured the parallax of well over a billion stars. The shift is so small that no one measured it until 1838. Even the nearest star's shift is only about the width of a coin seen from 6 or 7 kilometres away.
examples: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the Sun, is about 4.2 light-years away, and its parallax is about 0.77 arc-seconds, a tiny fraction of a degree.
A surveyor measuring the width of a river without crossing it uses the same method, with a baseline along the bank.
For more distant stars, astronomers use other methods, such as the pulsing of Cepheid stars, which were found to be a yardstick by Henrietta Leavitt.
explanations.art: A thumb in front of a face seen from two eyes, beside the Sun with the Earth at opposite points of its orbit seeing a star shift against faraway stars.
explanations.context: This card explains how distances to stars are measured. The thumb and wall experiment shows the same idea.

explanations.concept: How bright a star looks and how bright it really is
explanations.definition: A star looks bright because it is near, because it is truly powerful, or both. Astronomers call the first apparent brightness and the second true brightness, or luminosity.
explanations.description: A candle two metres away can look brighter than a bright lamp across a road. Stars are the same. Sirius is the brightest star in our night sky, mostly because it is near, only about 8.6 light-years away. It gives out about 25 times as much light as the Sun. Canopus, called Agastya in India, is the second brightest and is about 310 light-years away. It must be truly powerful, about ten thousand times brighter than the Sun. Rigel in Orion is further still and gives out tens of thousands of times as much light as the Sun. To find true brightness, you need the distance first. In 1912, Henrietta Leavitt, an American astronomer working at Harvard, found that a type of pulsing star, the Cepheid, pulses more slowly if it is truly brighter. This allowed astronomers to find distances to stars too far for parallax. The Pole Star is a Cepheid.
examples: Alpha Centauri, the nearest bright star, is about 4.4 light-years away and is only a little more powerful than the Sun, yet it looks very bright because it is so close.
If the Sun were as far away as Canopus, it would be far too faint to see without a telescope.
Magnitudes are such that a difference of 5 steps means a star is 100 times as bright.
explanations.art: A near small lamp and a far huge lamp that look equally bright, with a ruler beside them, and a second picture where the far one is shown to be much bigger.
explanations.context: This card explains why bright-looking stars are not always the nearest or the most powerful.

explanations.concept: A star's colour shows its temperature
explanations.definition: The hotter a star's surface, the bluer its light. A red star is cooler than a yellow one, and a blue-white star is hotter still.
explanations.description: A piece of iron in a fire first glows dull red, then orange, then yellow, and a white-blue colour if it gets very hot. A star glows in the same way. A red star such as Antares, which Indian astronomers call Jyeshtha, has a surface of about 3,500 degrees Celsius. The Sun is a yellow-white star at about 5,500. Sirius and Rigel are blue-white, at 10,000 degrees or more. Fire shows a similar thing: the blue part of a gas flame is hotter than the yellow flame of a diya. Around 1900, Annie Jump Cannon at Harvard sorted the light of hundreds of thousands of stars by colour into a sequence of types, from the hottest to the coolest. In 1925, Cecilia Payne showed from this work that stars are made mainly of hydrogen and helium.
examples: Betelgeuse, called Ardra, is a red star in Orion. Rigel, in the opposite corner of Orion, is blue-white. You can see the difference on a clear night.
The thin wire in an old bulb glows yellow-white, and it is hotter than the coil of an electric heater, which glows red.
Red stars are usually cooler than the Sun. A red star can still be huge, as Betelgeuse is.
explanations.art: Orion with red Betelgeuse at one shoulder and blue-white Rigel at one foot, and a row of five star colours below with temperatures from cool to hot.
explanations.context: This card explains how astronomers learn a star's temperature from its colour alone.

explanations.concept: Planets and stars: who wanders, and who twinkles
explanations.definition: The planets are called wanderers because they move slowly against the stars. Stars twinkle because their light is bent by the moving air. Planets look like tiny discs, so they usually twinkle much less.
explanations.description: Starlight is a single tiny point when it reaches the top of our air. On the way down it passes through patches of air of slightly different temperature, which bend it one way and another. The point seems to flicker. A planet is a disc that is still very small to the eye, but its light comes from many points on the disc. Their flickers mostly average out, so the planet shines steadily. Over days and months, planets wander along the ecliptic against the stars. Venus is seen only near sunrise or sunset. Jupiter and Saturn move slowly. Mars is slightly red. A bright, steady dot is probably a planet. Stars near the horizon twinkle more than overhead stars, because their light crosses more air.
examples: Venus looks like a very bright, steady star in the west after sunset, or in the east before sunrise.
A star low in the sky flashes red, green and blue as the air bends its colours differently.
Mars is called Mangal in many Indian languages and Sevvai in Tamil, and its reddish colour is visible by eye.
explanations.art: Starlight passing through bumpy layers of air to a child's eye and flickering, next to a planet's wider disc of light that stays steady.
explanations.context: This card explains how to tell a planet from a star, and why twinkling happens.

explanations.concept: The Pole Star will not always be the Pole Star
explanations.definition: The Earth's axis slowly wobbles like a spinning top, tracing a circle in the sky once in about 26,000 years. So the star nearest the north pole changes over time. This wobble is called precession.
explanations.description: Because of precession, the north pole points to different stars at different times. About 4,700 years ago, a star called Thuban was the pole star, around the time the great pyramids of Egypt were built. In about 12,000 years, the bright star Vega will be near the pole. Precession also moves the Sun's place among the stars. The Sun enters the constellation of Capricorn, called Makara, later than it did long ago. In the Indian star-based calendar, the Sun enters Makara around 14 January, which is the festival of Makar Sankranti or Pongal. That date was close to 21 December about 1,600 years ago, and it keeps moving later by about one day every 72 years. The star signs of western astrology, based on the seasons, are now about 24 degrees, or about 24 days, ahead of the Indian star-based signs.
examples: Polaris will be at its closest to the pole around the year 2100, and then slowly drift away.
In ancient Egypt, Thuban was the star around which the northern sky turned.
Pongal on 14 January and the winter solstice on 21 December were once the same day and are now about 24 days apart.
explanations.art: A spinning top wobbling, with a circle in the sky traced by its axis and small labels for Thuban, Polaris and Vega along the circle with their years.
explanations.context: This card explains why even the Pole Star changes over thousands of years.

explanations.concept: How did the people of the Pacific find tiny islands?
explanations.description: Long before there were maps, compasses or ships with instruments, people crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific Ocean and settled on tiny islands. How they found those islands has been argued about for a hundred years. We know that traditional navigators carry a star compass in their heads: they remember the points on the horizon where dozens of stars rise and set. They also watch the swell of the sea, the flight of birds and the shape of clouds over an island. In 1976, a double-hulled canoe called Hokulea sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti, about 4,000 kilometres, guided by Mau Piailug, a navigator from the island of Satawal, without any instrument. But many scientists still argue about how settlers first crossed the ocean thousands of years ago.
examples: Stars that rise at a particular point on the horizon rise at the same point every night, so a navigator can steer by a star close to the horizon and then change to the next one as it climbs.
A navigator can find latitude by noting which stars pass directly overhead. The star Arcturus, called Hokule'a by Hawaiians, passes over Hawaii.
Birds that go out to sea to fish in the day and return at night point towards land.

perspectives.who: Andrew Sharp, a New Zealand historian, in 1956
perspectives.explanation: Early voyages were mostly by accident. Canoes were blown off course by storms and wound up on islands by luck. Navigators could not have steered such long distances without instruments.

perspectives.who: David Lewis, Ben Finney and the crew of Hokulea, from the 1960s and 1970s
perspectives.explanation: The Pacific peoples crossed on purpose. The 1976 voyage proved that a trained navigator can steer across thousands of kilometres using only stars, swells and birds, so it could have been done long ago.

explanations.art: A double-hulled canoe under a sky full of stars, with a navigator at the steering paddle looking at a star near the horizon and a bird flying ahead.
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument: how did the first Pacific voyagers find their way across the open ocean?

agreed.text: The Earth spins once in about 24 hours, and that is why the stars, the Sun and the Moon seem to cross the sky each day.
agreed.evidence: Long photographs of the night sky show every star as an arc of the same angle. A Foucault pendulum swings in a line that turns slowly through the day, which shows that the floor under it is turning.

agreed.text: The Pole Star's height above the horizon equals the observer's latitude, to within about one degree.
agreed.evidence: Sailors and surveyors have measured it for centuries, and it matches latitude from maps and from satellite positioning. It works because the star is so far away that its light reaches the whole Earth along the same direction.

agreed.text: Different stars are up at night in different seasons because the Earth goes round the Sun.
agreed.evidence: A given star rises about 4 minutes earlier every night, which adds up to a full circuit in a year. This is exactly what is expected if the Earth moves round the Sun once in a year.

agreed.text: The distances to the nearest stars can be measured by parallax, and they are enormous.
agreed.evidence: Friedrich Bessel first measured the parallax of a star in 1838. Today the Gaia spacecraft has measured the parallax of well over a billion stars, and its distances agree with older methods.

agreed.text: A star's colour shows how hot its surface is: red stars are cooler and blue-white stars are hotter.
agreed.evidence: In the early 1900s, Annie Jump Cannon at Harvard sorted the light of hundreds of thousands of stars into a sequence by colour. Physicists then showed that the sequence follows the temperature of the stars' surfaces.

agreed.text: Henrietta Leavitt's discovery of the Cepheid stars gave astronomers a way to measure distances far beyond the reach of parallax.
agreed.evidence: In 1912 she found that Cepheids which pulse more slowly are truly brighter. The rule has been checked on Cepheids whose distances are known from parallax.

agreed.text: Stars twinkle because of the Earth's moving air, not because the stars themselves flicker.
agreed.evidence: Stars photographed from space telescopes shine steadily. Stars seen low on the horizon, through more air, twinkle the most.

challenging.claim: The stars are fixed to a great sphere that turns round the Earth once a day.
challenging.who: Many ancient Greek and Indian astronomers, and most people for about 2,000 years
challenging.for: All the stars keep their places relative to each other as they cross the sky. A single turning sphere is a simple way to picture it.
challenging.against: Parallax shows that the stars are at hugely different distances, so they are not on one shell. Spacecraft like Gaia have mapped the stars in three dimensions.
challenging.context: This card is about the old picture of the sky as a turning dome of stars.

challenging.claim: If the Earth went round the Sun, the stars would seem to shift during the year. Nobody sees a shift, so the Earth must be standing still.
challenging.who: Tycho Brahe, a Danish astronomer of the 1500s, and many careful scientists before him
challenging.for: The argument is sound. If the Earth did move, a near star would show parallax against the far ones, just as your thumb jumps when you swap eyes. Tycho measured stars more exactly than anyone in his time and saw no shift.
challenging.against: The stars are much farther away than Tycho could imagine, so the shift is far smaller than his instruments could detect. In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured it.
challenging.context: This card is about a very good argument that turned out to rest on a wrong guess about the distance of the stars.

challenging.claim: The Pole Star is the brightest star in the sky.
challenging.who: A very common idea, even among adults
challenging.for: It is famous, it is always in the same place, and it is used to find north, so it seems it must be special.
challenging.against: The Pole Star is about as bright as the stars of the Saptarishi. Dozens of stars look brighter, including Sirius, which is about 20 times brighter to the eye.
challenging.context: This card is about a mix-up between being important and being bright.

challenging.claim: The stars that look the brightest are the nearest ones.
challenging.who: A natural guess, and one most children make
challenging.for: A lamp looks brighter when it is closer. Some of the brightest stars, such as Sirius, are indeed among the nearest.
challenging.against: Canopus looks bright but is about 310 light-years away, while many stars much nearer to us are too faint to see. How bright a star looks depends on both its distance and how much light it gives out.
challenging.context: This card is about a rule that is partly true, and what it leaves out.

challenging.claim: The paintings in the cave of Lascaux, in France, about 17,000 years old, show the Pleiades and the stars of Taurus.
challenging.who: Some archaeologists and astronomers, including Michael Rappenglueck, since the 1990s
challenging.for: A cluster of dots on the shoulder of a painted bull looks like the Pleiades in the right place. If true, people were mapping the sky a very long time ago.
challenging.against: Dots appear all over the cave walls, and it is easy to see patterns in them. There is no way to check what the painters meant.
challenging.context: This card is about a bold idea of how old our star-watching is, which cannot yet be proved or ruled out.

big_questions.q: Your two eyes see a pencil in two slightly different places, and the gap tells you how far away it is. Is a disagreement between two views a mistake, or is it a tool?
big_questions.hint: Think of the thumb jumping. If both eyes saw exactly the same, could you tell what is near and what is far?

big_questions.q: You stand on a spinning planet but you feel perfectly still. How can you tell it is the Earth that turns, and not the sky?
big_questions.hint: Think of a train at a station that seems to move when the train beside it starts. What would you look for to decide?

big_questions.q: The Pole Star's height tells you how far north you are. What else around you tells you where you are, even without a map?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Sun at noon, the length of a day, which plants grow nearby, or which way the rain comes from.

big_questions.q: People crossed the Pacific, with no instruments, by watching stars, swells and birds. What does that tell us about how much a person can learn by watching carefully?
big_questions.hint: A navigator can hold hundreds of star paths in memory. How might they have learned them, and how do you pass such knowledge on?

big_questions.q: A star looks bright. How can you tell whether it is bright because it is near or because it is truly powerful?
big_questions.hint: You would need its distance first. How might you find that, and what does that tell you about how knowledge is built up?

big_questions.q: The Pole Star will not stay the Pole Star. What other things that seem permanent are only changing too slowly for us to notice?
big_questions.hint: Think of a mountain, a river's course, or the Moon's distance. How slowly can something change and still be real?

big_questions.q: The planets are called wanderers because they seem to wander among the stars. Which is really wandering, the planet or the Earth we watch from?
big_questions.hint: Think about the train that seemed to move at the station. What does your own motion add to what you see?

big_questions.q: Most children in big cities never see the Milky Way. What do you think is lost when the night sky is hidden by lights?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the sky gave people: time, direction, stories, and the feeling of being very small. Can anything replace that?

story.title: The Star That Climbed
story.note: Meenakshi, Ammamma, Mr Das and Mrs Jayanthi, the train journey and the halt in the dark are made up. The science is real. The height of the Pole Star above the northern horizon equals the observer's latitude, and a fist at arm's length covers about 10 degrees. The kamal is a real navigating tool used by sailors in the Indian Ocean. Mrs Jayanthi's grandfather, who used one, is made up.
text: Meenakshi was nine, and she had never been further north than Madurai. Now she and her grandmother, Ammamma, were going all the way to Delhi on the long train, for her cousin Leela's wedding. It would take two nights and almost three days.

They climbed aboard at Kanyakumari in the evening. On the platform, Ammamma pointed over the roofs to the north. 'There, very low, just above the trees. That is Dhruva, the Pole Star. In the old story, Dhruva was a boy who asked for a place in the sky that would never move.'

'It never moves,' agreed Meenakshi. 'Our teacher says all the other stars go round it.' 'Mm,' said Ammamma. 'But keep watching it on this journey. You may see it climb.' Meenakshi laughed. 'It cannot climb if it never moves!'

She had her notebook and her school atlas in her bag. In class she had learned that a fist held out at arm's length covers about ten degrees of sky. At a halt that night she stood at the door of the train and held her fist up against the star. It sat on top of her fist, no higher. She wrote: Kanyakumari, less than one fist.

The next day the train rolled north through Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. Meenakshi played cards with the man in the seat opposite, Mr Das, a retired schoolteacher from Kolkata, who was going to Delhi for an important meeting. That evening, near Hyderabad, she checked the star again. Nearly two fists. She wrote it down.

On the second night, the train stopped in the dark. It did not stop at a station. There were no lights outside, only the sound of crickets and the long hum of the engine waiting. One hour passed, and then another. The lights in the compartment flickered and went out.

'Where are we?' said Mr Das, getting more and more worried. 'I have to reach Delhi by morning. Nobody says anything. We could be anywhere.' Ammamma shrugged. 'We are on a train, in India, in the dark. That is all I know.'

Meenakshi had an idea. She slid open the door a little and looked north. The Pole Star was clearly higher than it had been. She held her fist against it, then another fist on top, and then a little more. 'Two fists and a bit,' she whispered. 'About twenty-three degrees.'

She fetched her atlas and found the lines of latitude. The line for twenty-three degrees passed through the middle of India. 'Ammamma,' she said, 'I think we are near Bhopal, or just before it.' Mr Das laughed, not unkindly. 'A girl cannot find a train with a star.'

Just then, a torch beam came down the corridor. It was Mrs Jayanthi, the ticket examiner. 'Madam,' said Meenakshi, 'are we close to Itarsi?' Mrs Jayanthi stopped. 'Who told you that?' 'The Pole Star did,' said Meenakshi. 'It is two fists and a bit high. My atlas says that is the latitude of Itarsi or Bhopal.'

Mrs Jayanthi looked at her for a long moment. 'About twenty kilometres before Itarsi,' she said. 'We are waiting for a goods train to clear the line.' She smiled. 'My grandfather sailed dhows out of Mandvi in Gujarat. He used a kamal: a little wooden card on a knotted string. He held the string in his teeth, put the card at arm's length, and lined its edge up with the Pole Star. The knot told him the latitude. He never needed a map.'

Mr Das stared out of the door into the dark. 'So the star told you where we were,' he said slowly, 'and it never moved at all.' 'Dhruva did not climb,' said Meenakshi. 'We did. Each degree we go north, the star is one degree higher. That is the same number as the latitude in my atlas.'

The train gave a jolt and began to move. By the time they reached Delhi the next morning, Meenakshi had filled a page: less than one fist, nearly two, two and a bit. She drew a little arrow climbing up the page. It was still climbing.

That night on the terrace of Leela's building, Dhruva stood high above the water tanks. 'Look,' said Meenakshi. She held up her fist three times, one on top of the other, and it reached almost to Dhruva. 'In Kanyakumari it was hardly above my fist.' Leela, who was getting married the next morning and could not sleep, looked up. 'So did the star move?' she asked. 'No,' said Meenakshi. 'We did.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: the Pole Star's height above the northern horizon equals the observer's latitude. A traveller going north therefore sees it climb, though the star has not moved. Meenakshi measures the height with her fist, which covers about ten degrees at arm's length, and uses her atlas to turn it into a place. What changes is the viewpoint, not the star. This is also the idea behind parallax: a change of viewpoint changes what we see in a way we can measure.
ask: Why did the Pole Star look higher each night as the train went north?
How did Meenakshi find out roughly where the train had stopped?
When Meenakshi said 'We did', what did she mean?
Why would the Pole Star look even lower from the southern tip of India than it does from Chennai?

roots.context: We have measured how the sky turns, how high the Pole Star stands, and how the jump of a thumb tells distance. Now we ask what these tell us about seeing, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the thumb test, your two eyes saw the pencil in two places. The size of that gap told you how far away the pencil was. So a difference between two viewpoints is not an error to remove. It is how distance is measured, and astronomers use the Earth's yearly path as their pair of eyes.
deep_truth.habit: We often think that when two people see the same thing differently, one must be wrong, and that the true view is the one from nowhere. But the difference between views can carry information that no single view has.
deep_truth.evidence: In the thumb test, the jump was large when the pencil was near and small when it was far, and a hidden pencil's distance could be read from its jump. In 1838, Bessel measured a star's tiny shift between two places in the Earth's orbit, and found it was about 11 light-years away.

three.who_am_i: You have two eyes a few centimetres apart. That small gap lets you tell how far away a cup is when you reach for it. You see depth because your two views are different.
three.what_is_life: A cat measuring a jump to a wall, a hawk diving at a mouse, and a child catching a ball all use two slightly different views of the same thing. For many animals, living well depends on comparing viewpoints.
three.what_is_this_world: We can measure the distance to a star because the Earth is not still. The planet we stand on is a moving pair of eyes, and the whole sky has depth because of it.

roots.thread: Two people can look at the same pencil and see it in different places. Two eyes do the same thing all the time. Instead of being confused, your brain uses the gap to make a picture with depth. Astronomers do the same on a vast scale. They look at a star in January and again in July from opposite ends of the Earth's orbit, and the small shift tells them how far away the star is. If the Earth stood still, or if we saw from only one place, the sky would be flat. The universe has depth for us because we see it from more than one place. A view from one point is never the whole story, and several views together can show something that none shows alone.

teachings.teaching: Truth is one. The wise speak of it in many ways.
teachings.link: Two eyes, or two points in the Earth's orbit, see one star in slightly different places. Putting the views together gives the one distance.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4 (the story of the blind men and the elephant)
teachings.teaching: Blind men each touched a different part of an elephant. One said it was like a pot, one like a fan, one like a plough. They began to quarrel, each sure that the others were wrong.
teachings.link: Each view was true of one part. The thumb test shows the gap between views is useful, and the whole picture is built from several views.

teachings.teaching: Whatever the thing, whoever says it, to see the truth in it is wisdom.
teachings.link: In the thumb test, the second eye does not contradict the first. It adds what the first could not show.

science.text: Parallax gives the distance to nearby stars, and it has been measured for well over a billion stars by the Gaia spacecraft.
Polynesian navigators could cross the open Pacific on purpose using stars, swells and birds. How the first settlers did it is argued about.
Whether the Lascaux paintings show the Pleiades is not known.

other_view.view: Parallax is simply geometry, and it contains no deeper lesson about viewpoints. A star has a distance whether anyone measures it or not. The difference between views is a tool we use because we are stuck in one place, and the best aim is a view from no particular place at all.

practice.title: One thumb, two eyes
practice.say: Hold your thumb out at arm's length. Close your left eye and look at your thumb against something far away. Now close your right eye and open your left. Watch your thumb jump. Breathe in slowly three times. Notice that you see the world in depth because your two eyes disagree a little.
practice.kid: Hold up your thumb. Close one eye, then the other. Watch the jump. Breathe slowly three times.

ask: When two people see the same thing differently, is one of them always wrong?
If you could see the sky from a planet round another star, what would you learn that you cannot learn from here?
Is a view from nowhere possible, or is every view from somewhere?
roots.art: A child holding up a thumb in front of a window, seen from the left eye and the right eye, with the two views side by side and a faint star behind the glass.

games.title: Spin the Sky: a game of the turning stars
games.context: This is a question game with a sky clock. A reader asks a question about how the sky turns, where the Pole Star stands, or how stars are measured, and players answer it.

setup.art: A round sky clock board with twelve numbered places round a circle and a drawn Pole Star in the middle, with a paper arrow pinned in the centre.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the sky clock and the paper arrow. Pin the arrow at the middle.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a face-down pile next to the sky clock and a score sheet with three names.
setup.caption: 2. Shuffle the cards into a pile with the questions facing up.

setup.art: A reader turning the paper arrow from the 12 to the 9 on the sky clock while the other players write their answers.
setup.caption: 3. For a clock question, show your answer by turning the arrow.

printables.title: A sky clock: 12 numbered places round a circle, with the Pole Star drawn at the middle
1 paper arrow, the line from the Pole Star to the two pointer stars of the Saptarishi, to pin at the middle of the sky clock
items: Paper arrow about 10 centimetres long, with a hole at one end for a pin or a finger to hold it at the middle

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a question on the front, and the answer on the back

items.f: CLOCK. At 8 pm the pointer stars point to 12 o'clock. Where do they point at 10 pm?
items.b: 11 o'clock. The sky turns 15 degrees an hour, so 2 hours is 30 degrees, which is one number on the clock, anticlockwise.

items.f: CLOCK. At 8 pm the pointer stars point to 12 o'clock. Where do they point at 2 am?
items.b: 9 o'clock. Six hours is 90 degrees, a quarter turn, which is three numbers back on the clock.

items.f: CLOCK. At 9 pm the pointer stars point to 3 o'clock. Where do they point at 3 am?
items.b: 12 o'clock. Six hours is a quarter turn anticlockwise, from the 3 back to the 12.

items.f: CLOCK. At 10 pm the pointer stars point to 6 o'clock. Where do they point at 4 am?
items.b: 3 o'clock. Six hours is a quarter turn, from the 6 back to the 3.

items.f: CLOCK. At 7 pm the pointer stars point to 9 o'clock. Where do they point at 1 am?
items.b: 6 o'clock. Six hours is a quarter turn, from the 9 back to the 6.

items.f: CLOCK. At midnight the pointer stars point to 4 o'clock. Where do they point at 6 am?
items.b: 1 o'clock. Six hours is three numbers back, from the 4 to the 1.

items.f: CLOCK. At 9 pm the pointer stars point to 12 o'clock. Where will they point at 9 pm tomorrow?
items.b: Back at 12 o'clock, or one degree past it. The sky makes one full turn in a day.

items.f: How many degrees does the sky turn in 1 hour? How many hours does it take to turn a quarter of a circle?
items.b: 15 degrees in 1 hour. A quarter circle is 90 degrees, and 90 divided by 15 is 6 hours.

items.f: Looking north, do the stars circle the Pole Star clockwise or anticlockwise?
items.b: Anticlockwise, the opposite way to the hands of a clock.

items.f: Why does the Pole Star seem to stay still while all the other stars circle it?
items.b: The Earth's axis points almost straight at it. As the Earth spins, the Pole Star stays in the same spot.

items.f: You are in Chennai, about 13 degrees north. About how high is the Pole Star above the northern horizon?
items.b: About 13 degrees, a little more than one fist at arm's length.

items.f: You are in Delhi, about 29 degrees north. About how high is the Pole Star above the northern horizon?
items.b: About 29 degrees, nearly three fists at arm's length.

items.f: You stand at the North Pole. Where is the Pole Star in the sky?
items.b: Straight overhead, at 90 degrees.

items.f: You stand on the equator. Where is the Pole Star in the sky?
items.b: On the northern horizon, at 0 degrees.

items.f: A traveller goes by train from Kanyakumari (8 degrees north) to Delhi (29 degrees north). By about how much does the Pole Star climb?
items.b: About 21 degrees, which is about two fists. 29 take away 8 is 21.

items.f: Is Orion in the night sky in June? Why or why not?
items.b: No. In June the Sun is near Orion in the sky, so Orion is up in the daytime and hidden by sunlight.

items.f: A star rises at 8 pm tonight. At about what time will it rise in one month?
items.b: About 6 pm. A star rises about 4 minutes earlier each day, which adds up to about 2 hours in a month.

items.f: In January the Sun is in front of Sagittarius. Which group of stars is highest at midnight?
items.b: Gemini, on the opposite side of the sky from the Sun.

items.f: Why are different stars seen at night in summer and in winter?
items.b: The Earth goes round the Sun, so at night we face a different part of space in each season.

items.f: A pencil near your nose jumps a lot when you swap eyes. A pencil at arm's length jumps less. What does a bigger jump tell you?
items.b: The pencil is nearer. The nearer a thing is, the bigger its parallax.

items.f: Why can you not see the parallax of a star by closing one eye and then the other?
items.b: Stars are so far away that the jump from a baseline of a few centimetres is far too tiny. Astronomers use the Earth's orbit, which is 300 million kilometres wide.

items.f: A red star and a blue-white star. Which has the hotter surface?
items.b: The blue-white star. The bluer a star, the hotter it is.

items.f: Canopus gives out about 400 times as much light as Sirius, yet Sirius looks brighter. Why?
items.b: Sirius is much nearer, only about 8.6 light-years away. Canopus is about 310 light-years away.

items.f: Two bright dots in the evening sky. One flickers and flashes colours. The other shines steadily. Which is more likely to be a planet?
items.b: The steady one. Stars twinkle because the air bends their pinpoint of light. A planet is a tiny disc and twinkles much less.

rules: Put the sky clock in the middle of the table and pin the paper arrow at its centre. Shuffle the 24 cards into a pile, question side up.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the question aloud. The reader does not show the back.
For a CLOCK card, the reader first turns the arrow to the starting number. Every other player then thinks, and turns a finger on the clock to show where the arrow will point.
For all other cards, the players say or write their answers. On the count of three, everyone shows their answer at once.
The reader turns the card over and reads the answer. A right answer scores 2 points. A player who also gives the reason in their own words scores 1 more.
The next player to the left becomes the reader. Play 12 cards for a short game, or all 24 for a long one. The player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.
Playing alone? Turn up one card at a time, write down your answer, then check the back. Keep your score, and try to beat it another day.
Two to four players is best. With more, play in teams that agree an answer before the reader turns the card.

flow.do: Cut out the sky clock, the paper arrow and the 24 cards. Fix the arrow in the middle with a paper fastener. A grown-up can push a drawing pin through it into clay instead. No pin? Hold the arrow at the middle with a fingertip. No printer? Draw the clock on paper, and have the reader read the questions from the list. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: This clock shows the sky as you look north. The Pole Star is in the middle. The stars turn round it, anticlockwise, 15 degrees every hour.
flow.kid: Cut out the clock, the arrow and the cards. Pin the arrow in the middle.
flow.context: This is the first step of Spin the Sky. You cut out the clock and the cards.

flow.do: Play the first four cards that say CLOCK. After each one, ask which way the arrow turned and by how many numbers.
flow.say: Set the arrow where the card says. Which way do the stars go? Every two hours, the arrow moves back one number. Where does it point now?
flow.kid: Set the arrow. The stars go anticlockwise. Two hours moves it back one number.

check.q: At 8 pm the pointer stars point to 12 o'clock. At 2 am, where do they point?
check.why: Six hours is a quarter turn, and the stars turn anticlockwise, the opposite way to a clock hand. So from 12 the arrow goes back to 9. If you picked 3 o'clock, you turned the arrow the way a clock hand goes.

flow.parent: If a child turns the arrow the wrong way, ask them to look at a real clock and then to turn the arrow the opposite way. The stars circle anticlockwise when you look north.

flow.do: Play four cards about the Pole Star's height and the places in India. Show the answer with your fist held out at arm's length.
flow.say: A fist at arm's length covers about 10 degrees. Hold up your fist for Chennai. How many fists high is the Pole Star? Now do Delhi.
flow.kid: Use your fist for the height. Chennai is about one fist. Delhi is about three.

ask.q: Why is the Pole Star higher in Delhi than in Chennai?
good: Delhi is further north.
The Pole Star's height is the same as how far north you are.
As you go north, the Pole Star climbs.

flow.do: Play the rest of the cards you have time for, including the ones about seasons, distance, colour and brightness. Keep the score.
flow.say: Keep going. Your turn to read. Try to give the reason for your answer, not only the answer. A reason is worth an extra point.
flow.kid: Take turns to be the reader. Give a reason as well as an answer.
flow.parent: Younger children can play for the answers only. Older children can aim for the extra point for the reason.

flow.do: Add up the points. Ask which question was the hardest, and which idea they would like to try for real.
flow.say: Which question was hardest? Which idea would you like to test on a real night, with real stars?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which question was hardest? What would you like to try outside?

ask.q: Which of the ideas in the game could you check with real stars?
good: How far the stars turn in an hour.
How high the Pole Star is.
Which stars are up in which month.

flow.context: This is the last step of Spin the Sky. You count the score and think about which ideas to check for real.

experiments.title: The Jump of Your Thumb: can a pencil's jump tell you how far away it is?
experiments.question: When you close one eye and then the other, a pencil seems to jump against a far wall. How does the size of the jump change with how far the pencil is from your nose? Can you use the jump to find a hidden pencil's distance?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the pencil jump more when it is close to your nose, or when it is far away? And if you bring it twice as close, will the jump be the same, twice as big, or four times as big? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Stand on the same spot, 3 metres from the wall, every time. Use the same pencil, held upright, with its tip lined up with the same mark on the wall strip. Use the same two eyes, one at a time. Only the distance from your nose to the pencil changes. Measure each distance with a string, and do each one twice.
results_table: Distance from my nose to the pencil (cm)
Number on the wall strip with my right eye only
Number on the wall strip with my left eye only

materials.item: a long piece of masking tape, about 1.5 metres, to stick on a wall
a marker pen
a pencil with a pointed tip
a string about 1.2 metres long and a ruler or tape measure
a bare wall with a clear 3 metre space in front of it, and a second piece of masking tape for the floor
a grown-up helper (or, with 2 to 4 children, a second child), and a notebook for the results

experiments.safety: Hold the pencil with the sharp tip pointing up and away from faces. Clear the floor so that nobody trips while stepping back from the wall.

schedule.what: Guess. Mark a wall strip. Measure the pencil's jump at 25, 50 and 100 centimetres. Use your results to find the distance of a pencil hidden at a secret distance.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then draw a line graph with the distance across the bottom and the jump up the side. Write down how close your guess for the hidden pencil came.
experiments.context: In this experiment you measure how far a pencil seems to jump when you swap eyes, at three distances. You then use your results to guess the distance of a hidden pencil. It is how astronomers first measured the distance to a star.

setup.art: A long strip of masking tape stuck along a wall at eye height, with a mark every 5 centimetres and numbers every 10 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Stick a 1.5 metre strip on the wall at eye height. Mark every 5 centimetres.

setup.art: A child standing on a taped spot on the floor exactly 3 metres from the wall, with a measuring tape stretched between the floor mark and the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Mark a spot on the floor 3 metres from the wall.

setup.art: A child holding a pencil upright at arm's length with one eye shut, looking at the wall strip behind the tip of the pencil.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the pencil at arm's length. Close one eye. Read the number behind the tip.

setup.art: The same child with the other eye shut, and the number behind the pencil's tip now far from the first number.
setup.caption: 4. Swap eyes and read the number again. The difference is the jump.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a pencil at a secret distance from a child's nose, with a string measure hidden behind a cloth.
setup.caption: 5. The grown-up holds the pencil at a secret distance. Use your jump to guess the distance.

flow.do: Show your child the pencil and the wall. Ask them to close one eye, then the other, with the pencil at arm's length. Then ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Look at the pencil against the wall. Close one eye, then the other. It seems to jump. If I bring the pencil twice as close, will it jump the same, twice as much, or four times as much? Why?
flow.kid: Swap eyes. Does the pencil jump? Guess what happens when it is closer. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will jump more, or less, when it is closer?
good: Closer things look different from each eye.
The pencil is nearer to my eyes so the two views are more different.
It will be the same, because it is the same pencil.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Many children say twice as big, and that is close to the truth.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Jump of Your Thumb. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: Stick the masking tape along the wall at your child's eye height. Make a mark every 5 centimetres and write a number at every 10 centimetres, with 0 at the left end. Stick a second piece of tape on the floor, 3 metres from the wall. Make three string marks at 25, 50 and 100 centimetres from one end.
flow.say: This strip is a ruler on the wall. The mark on the floor is where you will stand every time. The string has three knots for the three distances.
flow.kid: Mark the wall like a ruler. Mark a spot 3 metres from it.
flow.parent: The strip should have the pencil's tip in the middle of it when you stand on the spot. A strip 1.5 metres long is enough for the largest jump. The string measures the distance from nose to pencil. One end touches the nose.
flow.context: In this step you make a ruler on the wall and a spot to stand on.

flow.do: Stand on the spot. Hold the pencil upright with its tip at 25 centimetres from your nose, using the string. Close your left eye and read the number behind the tip. Close your right eye and read the number again. Write both numbers and the jump. Do it twice. Then do 50 centimetres, then 100 centimetres with your grown-up holding the pencil.
flow.say: Hold the pencil still. Look with your right eye only. What number is behind the tip? Now your left eye only. What is it now? What is the difference?
flow.kid: Right eye only. Read the number. Left eye only. Read the number. Subtract.
flow.parent: Expect the jump to be about 55 to 65 centimetres at 25 centimetres, about 25 to 30 at 50, and about 10 to 12 at 100. Your numbers will differ because eyes are different distances apart. If the numbers wander, rest your elbow on a table or ask your helper to hold the pencil. A jump of zero means you moved your head. With 2 to 4 children, give out jobs: one holds the pencil at the knot of the string, one stands on the spot and reads, one writes in the table. Swap after each distance so everyone reads once, then compare tables. Eyes are set different distances apart, so each child's numbers will differ, but the pattern (nearer means bigger jump) will be the same. These numbers are typical for a child; a grown-up's eyes are further apart, so the jumps will be a little bigger. Keep your head still: rest your chin on a chair back if it helps.

flow.do: Look at the three jumps together. Ask what happens to the jump each time the pencil is brought twice as close.
flow.say: From 100 centimetres to 50, the distance was halved. What happened to the jump? And from 50 to 25?
flow.kid: Half the distance. Look at the jump. What happens?

check.q: When the pencil was brought to half the distance from your nose, what happened to the jump?
check.why: The nearer the pencil, the bigger the jump. When the distance was halved, the jump roughly doubled. If you picked 'the same', check your numbers again. If you picked 'smaller', you may have swapped the near and the far rows.

flow.do: Turn your back. Your grown-up holds the pencil at a secret distance from your nose, between 30 and 90 centimetres. They measure it with the string and keep the number hidden. You stand on the spot, measure the jump, and use your table to guess the distance. Then your grown-up shows the string.
flow.say: I have put the pencil at a secret distance. Measure its jump. Look at your table. Is the jump bigger or smaller than at 50 centimetres? So is the pencil nearer or farther? Make your best guess.
flow.kid: Measure the jump of the hidden pencil. Use your table to guess how far it is.
flow.parent: If the jump is 40 centimetres, it is between 28 (at 50) and 60 (at 25), so the pencil is between 25 and 50 centimetres away, a bit nearer to 50, so about 38. A guess within 10 centimetres is very good. Swap roles if you like. With several children, one child hides the pencil and measures the string while the others each measure the jump, guess, and then compare guesses.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then ask about the stars.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Now, if a star is a million times further than the wall, how much would it jump?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a nearer thing jumps more, so the jump can tell the distance. What I saw: at 25 centimetres the jump was about 60, at 50 about 28, at 100 about 11. Why: each eye sees the pencil from a slightly different place, so it lines up with a different spot on the wall, and the nearer it is, the more the two views differ. For the stars, the jump is so tiny from the gap between our eyes that nobody can see it. Astronomers look from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit, 300 million kilometres apart, and measure a tiny shift.

experiments.title: The Turning Sky: how far does a star move in one hour?
experiments.question: If you watch a star for an hour, how far does it move across the sky, measured in fists at arm's length? Does it move the same amount each half hour?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In one hour, will a star move about half a fist, about one and a half fists, or about five fists? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Stand on exactly the same spot every time, marked with chalk or tape. Use the same arm, held straight, and the same fist. Measure from the same fixed roof edge to the same star each time. Only the time changes.
results_table: Fists from the roof edge to the star

materials.item: a balcony, terrace or open window with a clear view of the sky towards the east or the west, and a fixed roof edge or wall top below the star
chalk or tape to mark where you stand
a bright star or planet, found with a sky map such as Stellarium Web (a grown-up uses the phone, with the screen dimmed)
a watch or phone clock, and a notebook and pencil
a red torch, or a phone torch covered with red cellophane, to read your notes
a grown-up to stay with you

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays with the child outside at night. On a terrace, keep well away from the edge. Do not use a bright white light, which spoils your night vision.

schedule.what: Guess. Choose a star and mark your spot. Measure at the start, after 30 minutes and after 60 minutes. Work out how far the sky turns in an hour.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw the roof edge and the star at the three times, on one page, with arrows to show the way the star moves.
experiments.context: In this experiment you watch a star move across the sky over an hour and measure how far it goes with your fist. It shows that the sky turns at a steady rate, because the Earth is spinning.

setup.art: A child on a balcony at dusk holding a fist at arm's length between a fixed roof edge and a bright star, with chalk marks on the floor for the feet.
setup.caption: 1. Mark your spot. Count the fists from the roof edge to the star.

setup.art: Three small drawings of the same roof edge, with a star one fist above it, then two fists, then three.
setup.caption: 2. Measure again after 30 minutes and after 60 minutes.

setup.art: A notebook page with three times and the numbers of fists, and an arrow from the first measurement to the last.
setup.caption: 3. Work out how many fists the star moved in an hour.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: Fists from the roof edge to the star

flow.do: Ask for the guess and the reason before you go outside. Write it down.
flow.say: The stars seem to move across the sky. If we watch one star for an hour, how far will it move? Half a fist, one and a half fists, or five fists? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How far does a star move in one hour? Half a fist? One and a half? Five? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will move that far?
good: It crosses the whole sky in one night, so it should move a lot.
I cannot see it moving, so it must be slow.
The Moon moves about that much.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. This takes about an hour on the clock, with two waits of 30 minutes. Use the waits for tea or the drawing. If the night is cloudy, as is common in the monsoon, wait for a clear night.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Turning Sky experiment. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: Go outside after dark with your grown-up. Choose a bright star or planet in the east or the west, at least three fists above a fixed roof edge. Mark your standing spot with chalk. Hold out your arm and count the fists from the roof edge to the star. Write the time and the number.
flow.say: Stand on the chalk mark. Hold out your arm straight and make a fist. Count the fists up from the roof edge to the star. Write the time and the number.
flow.kid: Stand on your mark. Hold out your fist. Count the fists to the star.
flow.parent: Choose a star in the east or the west, not in the south, because stars there move mostly sideways. If you cannot find a bright star, use the Moon. A grown-up can point to Venus, Jupiter or Sirius using the sky map. If it is cloudy tonight, open Stellarium Web and watch the time slider, which shows the same turning.
flow.context: In this step you choose a star and measure how high it is above a roof edge.

flow.do: Draw the roof edge and the star in your notebook, with the first measurement. Then go inside or sit down for 30 minutes.
flow.say: Draw what you see. Where do you think the star will be in half an hour? Draw a small cross there.
flow.kid: Draw the star and the roof edge. Draw where you think the star will be soon.
flow.wait: Leave it for 30 minutes before the second measurement.

flow.do: After 30 minutes, stand on the same mark. Hold out your fist. Count the fists from the roof edge to the star again. Write the time and the number.
flow.say: Back to your mark. Same arm, same fist. Count the fists to the star. Did it move? Which way?
flow.kid: Back to your mark. Count the fists again. Did the star move?
flow.wait: Leave it for 30 minutes before the third measurement.
flow.parent: If the star was in the west, it will be lower, nearer to the roof edge. If it was in the east, it will be higher. Expect a change of about three-quarters of a fist in the half hour. Your fist counts are only good to about a quarter of a fist, so do not worry if the half-hour change is between half and one fist.

flow.do: After another 30 minutes, measure a third time. Work out the change since the first measurement.
flow.say: Last measurement. Same spot, same fist. Now take away your first number from this one. How many fists did the star move in one hour?
flow.kid: Count the fists one more time. Take away the first number. How far did the star go?

check.q: The star moved about one and a half fists in one hour. A fist is about 10 degrees. About how many degrees did it move?
check.why: One and a half fists is 1.5 times 10, which is 15 degrees. This matches the rate at which the Earth spins, 360 degrees in 24 hours, which is 15 degrees an hour. If you picked 1 degree, you may have counted a fist as one degree. A fist is about ten.

flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each child counts with their own fist and writes their own table. Compare: a child's fist at arm's length is a little smaller than 10 degrees, so a child may count nearer 1.8 fists than 1.5. Counts differ a little, but all show the same steady turn. One child can be the timekeeper.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then do the sum: how many hours for a full circle?
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think the star moved? If the sky turns 15 degrees every hour, how many hours does it take to go all the way round, 360 degrees?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the sky turns at a steady rate of about one and a half fists an hour. What I saw: at the start the star was 3 fists from the roof edge, and at the end 1 and a half. Why: the Earth spins, so the stars seem to turn. The sum is 360 divided by 15, which is 24 hours. A full turn takes a day, because the Earth spins once a day.

experiments.title: How High Is the Pole Star? Measure your latitude from the sky
experiments.question: How many degrees above the northern horizon is the Pole Star from where you live? Does it match your latitude on a map?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Is the Pole Star higher or lower in your city than in Delhi? Will it be about one fist high, two fists, or three? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same sighting tool for every reading. Stand in the same spot with a clear view to the north. Take five readings and use the middle one. Check the tool by day first, on something whose height you know.

materials.item: a plastic protractor from a geometry box
a drinking straw and a strip of tape
a thread about 30 centimetres long and a small weight such as a coin, a washer or a nut
a piece of stiff card or cardboard about the size of a postcard
a place at home with a clear view to the north, such as a balcony, terrace or window
a phone with Stellarium Web for a grown-up to check, a notebook, and a red torch

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays with the child outside at night. On a terrace, keep away from the edge. Do not look at the Sun with the tool in daytime. Never point the straw at the Sun, even by day; test it on buildings only.

schedule.what: Guess. Build the sighting tool. Test it by day on a roof. Find the Pole Star from the Saptarishi at night. Take five readings. Compare the middle one with your latitude.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Write your city's latitude from a map next to your answer. Draw the north horizon and the Pole Star with its height in degrees.
experiments.context: In this experiment you build a simple tool to measure the height of the Pole Star, and compare it with your latitude. It shows that the stars tell you where you are.

setup.art: A protractor taped to a card, a straw taped along its straight edge, and a thread with a coin hanging from the centre.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the straw along the flat edge. Hang the weight from the centre.

setup.art: A child pointing the straw at the top of a building across the road and reading where the thread crosses the scale.
setup.caption: 2. Test it by day. Sight the top of a building and read the thread.

setup.art: The Saptarishi with a line through its two pointer stars, and a child looking along the straw at a star at the end of the line.
setup.caption: 3. At night, find the Pole Star using the pointer stars. Sight it along the straw.

setup.art: A table of five readings with the middle one circled and a map of India beside it with a city dot and its latitude written next to it.
setup.caption: 4. Take five readings, pick the middle one, and compare with the latitude on the map.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results for a child in Chennai

flow.do: Ask for the guess and the reason. Write it down. Show the city list below.
flow.say: The Pole Star is about 8 degrees up in Kanyakumari, 13 in Chennai, and 29 in Delhi. Where do we live? Is the Pole Star higher or lower here than in Delhi? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Is the Pole Star higher here than in Delhi? Or lower? Guess. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will be lower, or higher, from where we live?
good: It depends on how far north we are.
I think it is higher in the north.
It is always in the same place, so it will be the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Latitudes, to the nearest degree: Kanyakumari 8, Thiruvananthapuram 9, Kochi 10, Madurai 10, Chennai 13, Bengaluru 13, Hyderabad 17, Mumbai 19, Kolkata 23, Ahmedabad 23, Jaipur 27, Delhi 29, Srinagar 34.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pole Star height experiment. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: Tape the straw along the flat edge of the protractor. Tape the protractor to the card. Tie the thread to the weight. Tape the other end of the thread to the middle of the flat edge, at the small hole or mark. Let the thread hang down freely over the scale.
flow.say: This is a clinometer. It measures how high something is above the ground. The straw is for looking along. The thread always hangs straight down. Where it crosses the scale tells us the angle.
flow.kid: Tape the straw to the flat edge. Hang the weight from the middle.
flow.parent: Hold it with the curved edge facing down. When the straw points flat at the horizon, the thread hangs along the 90 mark. The angle above the horizon is the difference between the scale reading and 90. A reading of 75, for example, means 15 degrees. If your protractor has two scales, use the one that reads 90 at the thread when the straw is level.
flow.context: In this step you build the sighting tool.

flow.do: In daylight, test the tool. Look along the straw at the top of a building across the road. Hold the tool still and read where the thread crosses the scale. Take away 90 and find the angle. Do it twice.
flow.say: Look along the straw at the top of the building. Hold still. Read the number the thread crosses. Take it away from 90. That is how many degrees above flat the roof is.
flow.kid: Look along the straw at a rooftop. Read the number. Take it from 90.
flow.wait: Do this by day. Do the night part when it is dark.

check.q: When you point the straw level at the horizon, what should the thread read?
check.why: The thread hangs straight down, and on a protractor the straight-down line is at the 90 mark. When the straw tilts up, the thread moves away from 90 by the same angle. If you picked 0, you may be looking at the wrong end of the scale.

flow.parent: Check the tool against something you know: stand as far from a wall as a marked spot on it is above your eye, and the thread should read about 45 degrees away from 90 (a 45-degree set square from the geometry box is a second check). Being 3 or 4 degrees out is normal.

flow.do: At night, go outside with your grown-up to a spot with a clear view to the north. Find the Saptarishi. Follow a line through the two pointer stars, Kratu and Pulaha, about five times the gap, to the Pole Star. Use a sky map if you cannot see it.
flow.say: Find the seven stars of the Saptarishi. Take the two stars at the outer edge of the bowl. Draw a line through them, and carry on about five gaps. The star at the end is the Pole Star. It is not very bright, so look carefully.
flow.kid: Find the Saptarishi. Follow the two pointer stars. The Pole Star is at the end.
