flow.parent: The Pole Star may be hard to see from a city, and low in the south of India it can be hidden by haze or buildings. Let your eyes get used to the dark for 15 minutes, and use a red torch only. If you cannot see it, use Stellarium Web to find where it is and look there. If it is cloudy tonight, try another night. The Saptarishi is low or even below the horizon in the evening in autumn and early winter, especially in the south. If you cannot see it, use Cassiopeia, the W-shaped group on the other side of the Pole Star, which is high on autumn and winter evenings: the Pole Star lies in line with the middle point of the W, a little way off.

flow.do: Look along the straw at the Pole Star. Hold the tool still and read where the thread crosses the scale. Take 90 away to find the angle. Do this five times. Use the middle reading.
flow.say: Hold the straw on the Pole Star. Keep it steady. Read the thread. Take away 90. Do it five times. We will use the middle number.
flow.kid: Look along the straw at the Pole Star. Read the thread. Do it five times.
flow.parent: Your readings may be off by 3 to 4 degrees, because a hand-held tool and a thread are not exact. Using the middle of five readings helps. The Pole Star is a little dim, so ask your grown-up to help line up the straw. With 2 to 4 children, one sights along the straw and one reads the thread, and a third writes; swap after each reading so everyone does every job, then compare each child's middle reading.

flow.do: Compare your middle reading with your city's latitude. Ask your child to say or write what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Our middle reading is close to our latitude. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think the Pole Star is that high here?
flow.kid: Is your answer close to your city's latitude? Say what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: A good answer: what I think, the Pole Star's height is the same as how far north I am. What I saw, I measured 14 degrees and Chennai's latitude is 13. Why: the Pole Star is so far away that its light comes in parallel to the Earth's axis everywhere, so the angle between the star and the ground depends only on how far north you are.

activities.title: The Year in a Room: a lamp, a ring of star cards and a walk round the Sun

materials.item: a table lamp with the shade taken off, or a yellow paper Sun on a chair, to stand in the middle of the room
12 pieces of paper about the size of a postcard, and a thick pen
masking tape, to fix the cards on the walls

a room about 3 metres across with clear floor, and a string about 1 metre long to mark the ring you walk on (hold one end at the foot of the lamp and mark the string's other end on the floor at 12 spots with small pieces of tape)
the list of twelve groups of stars written out by a grown-up

schedule.what: Guess. Make the twelve cards and put them on the walls round the lamp. Walk round the lamp one month at a time and read the sky behind you at midnight.

activities.safety: A grown-up switches the lamp on and off. A bare bulb can get hot, so use a cool LED bulb if you have one and nobody touches it. Keep the cord out of the ring you walk on so nobody trips.
activities.record: A table with the twelve months, the group of stars highest at midnight in each, and the group hidden by the Sun. Draw the lamp, the ring and the cards from above.
activities.context: In this activity you turn a room into the solar system, with a lamp as the Sun and twelve cards as the star groups round it. You walk round the lamp as the Earth does, and find out why the stars change with the seasons.

setup.art: Twelve postcard-sized cards taped on the walls of a room in a circle, each with the name of a group of stars, and a lamp standing in the middle of the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Put the lamp in the middle. Tape the twelve cards round the walls.

setup.art: A child standing on a string ring around the lamp with her back to it, facing a card on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Stand on the ring with your back to the lamp. The card ahead of you is your midnight sky.

setup.art: The same child a few steps further round the ring, now facing a different card, and a small calendar with the next month circled.
setup.caption: 3. Walk one step round the ring for each month. Read the next card.

flow.do: Ask your child to think about the night sky in January and in July. Ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: At midnight in January we look at some stars. At midnight in July, will we look at the same stars or different ones? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will the midnight stars in July be the same as in January? Guess. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the stars are the same, or different?
good: The stars are always there, so they are the same.
The Earth moves, so we look a different way.
The seasons are different, so the stars must be different.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many people think the stars are the same all year, or that the Earth tilts to see different ones.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Year in a Room. You guess before you walk.

flow.do: Stand the lamp in the middle of the room and switch it on. Write the twelve names on twelve cards. Tape them on the walls in a circle, going anticlockwise as seen from above. The order is Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpius, Sagittarius, Capricornus, Aquarius and Pisces. Use the string as a compass. Hold one end at the foot of the lamp. Stick 12 pieces of tape on the floor where the other end reaches. This makes a ring 1 metre from the lamp. Space the cards as evenly as the room allows, like the hours of a clock round the lamp.
flow.say: These are the twelve star groups along the Sun's path. Indians call them the rashis, such as Mesha, Vrishabha, Mithuna and Karka. The lamp is the Sun. You are the Earth, walking on the ring.
flow.kid: Put the lamp in the middle. Tape twelve cards round the walls, in order.
flow.parent: The twelve are Aries (Mesha), Taurus (Vrishabha), Gemini (Mithuna), Cancer (Karka), Leo (Simha), Virgo (Kanya), Libra (Tula), Scorpius (Vrischika), Sagittarius (Dhanu), Capricornus (Makara), Aquarius (Kumbha), Pisces (Meena). The Sun also passes through a thirteenth group, Ophiuchus, for about two weeks in December. We leave it out to keep the circle simple. A bare lamp bulb gets hot, so keep fingers off it.
flow.context: In this step you set up the room.

flow.do: Stand on the ring next to the card for Gemini, with your back to the lamp. You are looking at the midnight sky of January. Turn round to face the lamp. The card behind the lamp is Sagittarius, hidden by the Sun's glare. Then move along the ring, one card for each month, anticlockwise: Cancer for February, Leo for March, and so on. Each time, say which card you face at midnight and which card is hidden behind the lamp.
flow.say: Back to the lamp, you look at the night sky. Face the lamp, and you look at the Sun, with its star group behind it. Move one card each month. Which group is hidden in June?
flow.kid: Stand with your back to the lamp. The card ahead is the midnight sky. Move one card each month.
flow.parent: The group highest at midnight, by month: November Aries, December Taurus, January Gemini, February Cancer, March Leo, April Virgo, May Libra, June Scorpius, July Sagittarius, August Capricornus, September Aquarius, October Pisces. The group hidden by the Sun is the one on the opposite wall. This is rough, because the star groups are large and one is highest at midnight over about a month. It is a good guide. With 2 to 4 children, one child is the Earth and walks the ring, one says which card is ahead at midnight, one says which card is hidden behind the lamp, and one checks the table. Swap each month. Alone, do the walking and look the answer up in the table.

check.q: In July, Sagittarius is highest at midnight. Which group of stars is hidden by the Sun's glare that month?
options: Gemini, on the opposite side of the sky from Sagittarius
check.why: The Sun is on the opposite side of the Earth from the midnight sky. So the group directly across the circle from the midnight group is the one near the Sun. If you picked Sagittarius, you chose the midnight group. Scorpius is next to it, so it is up in the evening.

flow.do: Go back to your birth month, or the month it is now. Find the group of stars on the card ahead of you at midnight. Ask what you would look for outside, and what you would not see.
flow.say: It is the month of your birthday. Which group is highest at midnight? Which group do you never see in the night, because it is near the Sun?
flow.kid: Stand where it is your birth month. What is ahead at midnight? What is hidden?

ask.q: Why do we never see the group of stars that is near the Sun?
good: The Sun is so bright in the day that the stars near it are hidden.
Those stars are up in the day, not the night.
They are on the same side of the sky as the Sun.

flow.do: Ask where the full Moon would be, if it is always opposite the Sun. Link it to the Karthigai Deepam festival in November or December, when the full Moon is near Krittika, which is in Taurus.
flow.say: The full Moon is always on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun. Where would it be in your room? So in which group of stars is the full Moon in December?
flow.kid: The full Moon is opposite the Sun. Where is it in your room?

ask.q: In which group of stars is the full Moon in December, and why?
good: In Taurus, because that is the group highest at midnight in December.
The full Moon is opposite the Sun, so it is in the midnight group.
That is why Karthigai Deepam is lit when the full Moon is near Krittika.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Year in a Room. You use the room to place the full Moon among the stars.

activities.title: Ball, Straw and Far Star: why the Pole Star stands higher as you go north

materials.item: a ball about 20 centimetres across, such as a football, or a school globe
a bowl or a ring of clay to hold the ball steady on a table
a sticker or paper star, fixed to a wall about 3 metres from the table, at the same height as the ball
5 drinking straws, 5 small squares of stiff card about 4 centimetres across, and modelling clay or tape
a string about 40 centimetres long, a marker pen (on a shiny football it may smudge, so use small paper stickers or bits of tape for marks) and a ruler
a protractor from a geometry box

schedule.what: Guess. Set the ball so its north pole faces the far star. Mark five latitudes on it. Fix a straw and a flat card at each one, and measure the angle between them.

activities.record: A table with each place, its latitude, and the angle you measured between the straw and the card. Draw the ball with the straw and card at the equator, at Chennai and at the pole.
activities.context: In this activity you use a ball as the Earth and a star on the wall as the Pole Star. You find out how the angle of the Pole Star above the horizon changes with latitude.

setup.art: A ball held steady in a bowl on a table, with a marked north pole facing a paper star taped to a wall three metres away.
setup.caption: 1. Turn the ball so its north pole faces the star on the wall.

setup.art: A string laid from the equator to the pole over the surface of the ball, with a pen mark at each distance for a city.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the latitudes on the ball using the string.

setup.art: A straw stuck with clay on the ball, pointing at the far star, and a small square card lying flat against the ball beside it.
setup.caption: 3. At each mark, fix a straw pointing at the star and a flat card for the horizon.

setup.art: A protractor held at the corner where the straw meets the card, showing an angle of about thirteen degrees.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the angle between the straw and the card.

flow.do: Ask your child to imagine being a tiny person on the ball. Ask where the far star would be in the sky at the equator, and at the North Pole. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Imagine you are tiny, and standing on this ball, on the equator. Where would you see the Pole Star: overhead or on the horizon? And at the North Pole? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You are tiny, on the ball. Where is the star at the equator? At the pole? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the star is there?
good: At the pole it is straight above because the pole is the top.
At the equator it is on the horizon because it is far to the side.
I think it is the same everywhere, because the star is so far away.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many people guess that the star is higher at the equator, because the equator is the middle of the Earth.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ball, Straw and Far Star activity. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Fix the sticker on the wall at the same height as the ball. Put the ball in the bowl. Mark its north pole and south pole with the pen. Turn the ball until the north pole is the point nearest to the sticker. Then draw the equator, halfway between the poles, using the string.
flow.say: The star is very far away, so it is in the same direction from every part of the ball. We will point the ball's axis at it. The north pole must face the star.
flow.kid: Turn the ball so the north pole faces the star. Draw the equator.
flow.parent: If you have a globe with a stand, turn it so the north pole points at the star on the wall. For a football, find the stitching at the top and use that as the north pole. The ball can be held still with clay. The sticker is only 3 metres away rather than hundreds of light-years, but that is far enough for this model.
flow.context: In this step you set the ball so that its north pole faces the far star.

flow.do: Hold the string tight along the ball from the equator to the north pole, on the side facing you. Mark the length. This is 90 degrees of latitude. Work out where 8, 13 and 29 degrees go: the length times the latitude, divided by 90. Mark Kanyakumari at 8, Chennai at 13, Delhi at 29, and the pole at 90.
flow.say: The distance from the equator to the pole is 90 degrees of latitude. Say the string is 17 centimetres long. Chennai is 13 out of 90 of that. What is 17 times 13, divided by 90? About 2.5 centimetres.
flow.kid: Measure the string from the equator to the pole. That is 90 degrees. Find the marks.
flow.parent: For a football about 22 centimetres across, the quarter circle from the equator to the pole is about 17 centimetres. Then 8 degrees is about 1.5 centimetres, 13 degrees about 2.5, 29 degrees about 5.5. A hand calculator helps. Mark the equator itself as zero.

check.q: The string from the equator to the pole is 18 centimetres long and stands for 90 degrees. About where is the mark for 45 degrees?
check.why: 45 degrees is half of 90, so the mark is halfway along the string, at 9 centimetres. If you picked 4.5, you took a quarter instead of a half. 18 centimetres is the pole itself.

flow.do: At each mark, fix a straw with clay so that it points straight at the star on the wall. Next to it, fix a small square card lying flat against the ball, as the local horizon. Look at the ball from the side, so you see its edge. Measure the angle between the straw and the card with the protractor.
flow.say: At each place the card is the flat ground you would stand on, and the straw is the line to the star. How big is the angle between them? Write it down for each place.
flow.kid: Stick a straw at each mark, pointing at the star. Lay a card flat. Measure the angle.
flow.parent: Expect the equator to be about 0 degrees, Kanyakumari about 8, Chennai about 13, Delhi about 29 and the pole 90. It is hard to measure well, so your numbers may be off by 5 degrees, but the pattern should be clear. The angle grows with latitude. Because the star is so far away, every straw is parallel to the axis. To keep the straws pointing the same way, sight along each straw towards the sticker, or lay a ruler along the straw at the pole and set the others parallel to it. With 2 to 4 children, each child makes one or two places and measures the angle, and a third checks that the straw points at the sticker; then put the angles in one table and compare.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then ask what this means for a traveller going north.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happens? If you walked from Kanyakumari to Delhi, what would happen to the Pole Star?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the further north, the higher the Pole Star. What I saw: the angle was near 0 at the equator, near 13 for Chennai, and 90 at the pole. Why: the star is so far away that the line to it is the same direction everywhere, and the ground turns away from that line as you travel north. So the angle between ground and star equals the latitude. A graph of angle against latitude (a straight line up) is a good extra to draw if there is time.

activities.title: Twinkle and Colour: why stars flicker and what their colours show

materials.item: a phone with a torch, in a dark room or dim corridor about 4 metres long
a piece of kitchen foil about 10 centimetres square with a tiny pinhole pricked by a grown-up with a pin, and a second piece with a hole 1.5 centimetres wide cut by a grown-up
a heavy steel tawa or pan with a handle, heated by a grown-up on the stove and left there until it has cooled
a gas stove flame and a lit diya, lit by a grown-up
a phone or computer with Stellarium Web to look at the colours of Betelgeuse and Rigel in Orion

schedule.what: Guess. Look at a small light and a bigger light through the shimmering air above a hot tawa. Compare flame colours. Look at the colours of two stars in Orion.

activities.safety: A grown-up does all the heating, lights the stove and the diya, and moves the hot tawa. Keep the child at least 1.5 metres from the tawa, the flame and the diya. Do not carry the tawa: leave it on the stove ring where it was heated, with a dim light on beside it so it can be seen. Tie back long hair and keep loose clothes away from the flames. Let the tawa cool fully before it is touched or washed.
activities.record: Write which light flickered more, the tiny hole or the wider hole. Draw the gas flame and the diya flame and colour them. Write the colour of Betelgeuse and of Rigel, and which one is hotter.
activities.context: In this activity you make a small light twinkle by looking at it through hot, rising air, and you compare the colours of flames and stars. It shows why stars twinkle and planets mostly do not, and how colour shows temperature.

setup.art: A dim corridor with a phone torch covered by foil with a tiny hole at the far end, a hot steel tawa on a stand in the middle, and a child sitting at the near end.
setup.caption: 1. Cover the torch with foil with a tiny hole. Look past a hot tawa.

setup.art: The same corridor with the foil changed for one with a wider hole, and the light looking steady behind the hot tawa.
setup.caption: 2. Swap to the wider hole and look again.

setup.art: A blue gas stove flame and a yellow diya flame side by side with a child watching from a safe distance.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the colour of a gas flame and a diya flame.

setup.art: The constellation Orion on a phone sky map, with a red-orange star at one shoulder and a blue-white star at one foot.
setup.caption: 4. Find Betelgeuse and Rigel and compare their colours.

flow.do: Ask for the guess and the reason before you start.
flow.say: A star is a tiny point of light. A planet is a tiny disc. Which one do you think will flicker more when its light comes through moving air? Why?
flow.kid: A star is a point. A planet is a tiny disc. Which twinkles more? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one flickers more?
good: The point is smaller so it gets pushed about more.
The planet is bigger so it stays steady.
They both flicker the same, because they are both far away.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Twinkle and Colour. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up heats the tawa on a high flame for about 5 minutes. Then they turn off the gas and leave the tawa on the stove. Cover the torch with the pinhole foil and put it at the far end of the room. The line from your eyes to the torch must pass 3 to 5 centimetres above the tawa. Sit at the other end, with your eyes level with the warm air above the tawa. Watch the light. Then swap to the wider hole and watch again. Do this in the first few minutes after the gas is off.
flow.say: The air above the hot tawa rises and wobbles, like air high above the Earth. Watch the tiny light through it. Does it flicker? Now watch the wider light. Which one flickers more?
flow.kid: Watch the tiny light past the hot tawa. Does it flicker? Now the wider one.
flow.parent: Keep your child at least 1.5 metres from the hot tawa and do not let them touch it. The tawa stays hot for a long time. First check the shimmer: look at the edge of a wall or window over the tawa, and it should wobble. If it has stopped wobbling, the tawa has cooled, so reheat it. The tiny hole should usually flicker and shimmer clearly, but the effect is modest and depends on the room, so look for a difference, not a big show. A pinhole is also dimmer, which can make it look more flickery, so also try a hole of about 5 millimetres in between. With 2 to 4 children, one holds the torch at the far end while the others watch in turns and say 'flickering' or 'steady' for each hole; compare what everyone saw. The wider hole should look steadier. If you cannot see the difference, make the pinhole smaller or the wider hole larger. As an alternative with no heat, watch a far-off street lamp through the shimmer above a hot road on a sunny day.

check.q: The tiny hole flickered more than the wider hole. Which is like a star, and which is like a planet?
options: The tiny hole is like a star, and the wider hole is like a planet
The tiny hole is like a planet
check.why: A star is a point of light, so the moving air bends all of it together and it seems to flicker. A planet is a tiny disc made of many points, so the flickers of the different points average out. If you picked the planet for the tiny hole, think about which one is the point.

flow.do: A grown-up lights a gas stove ring and a diya. Look at both flames from a safe distance of about 1 metre. Notice the colours. Draw them.
flow.say: Look at the gas flame and the diya flame. Which has more blue in it? A hotter flame has more blue. Stars follow a similar pattern, but with the colour of their surface.
flow.kid: Look at the gas flame and the diya flame. Which is bluer? Colour them in.
flow.parent: Stay with your child by the stove, and keep hair and loose clothes away. Blue is a rough sign of heat in fire. The colour of a flame also depends on what is burning, so this is only a hint about stars. Stars are balls of hot gas glowing, and for them, colour is a good thermometer. The yellow in a diya flame is mostly glowing bits of soot, and a gas flame burns cleaner and hotter, so it is blue.

flow.do: Open a sky map and look at Orion. Find Betelgeuse at one shoulder and Rigel at one foot. Zoom in and look at the colour of each. If it is a clear winter night and Orion is up, look outside too.
flow.say: Betelgeuse is called Ardra in India. Rigel is at the opposite corner of Orion. What colour is each? Which one do you think is hotter? Why?
flow.kid: Find the two stars in Orion. What colour is each? Which is hotter?

ask.q: Which star is hotter, and how can you tell?
good: Rigel, because it is blue-white.
Betelgeuse is red, so it is cooler.
The bluer star is hotter.

flow.parent: Betelgeuse is red-orange and about 3,500 degrees Celsius at the surface. Rigel is blue-white and about 12,000 degrees. Both look quite similar in brightness to the eye, but the colours differ if you look carefully, especially with binoculars. On a clear night, if Jupiter or Venus is up, compare it with a star near it: the star twinkles more.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think the star-like light flickered more?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a point of light flickers more than a small disc. What I saw: the pinhole light shimmered and the wider one was steadier. Why: moving air bends a point of light as a whole, but for a disc the wobbles of many points cancel out. Stars are points and planets are tiny discs. Colour shows temperature: the bluer a star, the hotter.

projects.title: Dhruva's Clock: a month-long sky diary

materials.item: a notebook or sheets of paper, a pencil, a ruler and a protractor from a geometry box
a round plate or bowl to draw a clock face: make 12 big marks like the hours, then 4 small marks between each pair, to get 60 marks (an old clock face to copy helps)
a clear view to the north, from a balcony, terrace or window, at the same time each evening
a red torch, or a phone torch covered with red cellophane
a phone with Stellarium Web, for a grown-up to use if the sky is cloudy
a thread about 40 centimetres long with a coin or washer tied on, to hold up as a straight-down line

schedule.what: Make the diary page. Find the Pole Star and the Saptarishi. Draw the first sky clock at 8:30 pm.
At 8:30 pm, draw the sky clock again and compare with day 1.
At 8:30 pm, draw the sky clock again.
At 8:30 pm, draw the sky clock again.
Draw the last sky clock. Compare all five. Work out how far the sky has turned in a month.

projects.safety: A grown-up stays with the child outside at night. On a terrace or balcony, keep well away from the edge. Use a red torch, not a bright white light.
projects.record: Five sky clock drawings, one a week, each with the date and the minute-mark where the pointer stars' line falls. A final page saying how far the line moved in a month, and why.
projects.context: In this month-long project you draw the same part of the northern sky at the same time each week. You find out that the stars shift in a steady way through the seasons.

setup.art: A page with a circle drawn like a clock face with sixty small marks, a small star in the middle for the Pole Star, and the title Dhruva's Clock.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a clock face with 60 marks. Put the Pole Star at the middle.

setup.art: A child on a balcony at night looking north at the Saptarishi, with a line drawn from the Pole Star through the two pointer stars on a sketch.
setup.caption: 2. Find the Saptarishi. Draw the line from the Pole Star to the pointer stars.

setup.art: Five small clock faces in a row, each with a line from the centre that sits a little further anticlockwise than the one before.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the line again each week. Watch it move round.

flow.do: Draw a clock face with 60 small marks on a page, with 12 at the top. Put a small star in the middle for the Pole Star. At 8:30 pm, go outside with your grown-up. Find the Pole Star and the Saptarishi. Look at the line from the Pole Star through the pointer stars. Decide which minute-mark it points at, as if it were the minute hand of a clock. Draw the line and write the date.
flow.say: Think of the line from the Pole Star through the two pointer stars as the minute hand of a clock. Which number does it point at? Draw that line. We will draw it again every week at the same time.
flow.kid: Draw a clock. Find the Pole Star. Draw the line to the pointer stars.
flow.parent: Do the same each week at exactly the same clock time, from the same spot. If you are not sure of the minute-mark, hold your page up to the sky and compare. If it is cloudy, use Stellarium Web, set to your city, and move the date and time to show where the line points. The line will be higher or lower depending on the time, so the same hour each week matters. In a week the line moves back by about 1 minute-mark. The Saptarishi sits low in the north on autumn and early winter evenings and may be hidden, especially in the south of India. If so, use Cassiopeia, the W-shaped group on the other side of the Pole Star, and draw the line from the Pole Star to the middle point of the W; use the same group all month. To read the angle well, hold the thread with the weight at arm's length so it hangs straight down through the Pole Star, then use the protractor on your page to copy the angle of the pointer line from it. If a night is cloudy, draw on the next clear night and write the date: the sky shifts about 1 degree a day, so you can still compare. With 2 to 4 children, each draws their own clock and then compare; one holds the thread, one draws.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dhruva's Clock. You make the diary page and draw the first sky clock.

flow.do: A week later, at the same time, go out and draw the sky clock again. Compare with the first one. Has the line moved? Which way?
flow.say: Same time, same spot. Where does the line point tonight? Is it the same as last week, or has it moved?
flow.kid: Same time, same place. Draw the line again. Has it moved?
flow.wait: Wait 7 days before the second drawing.

ask.q: Did the line move? Which way, and by how much?
good: A little. It moved back.
About one minute-mark anticlockwise.
The stars are rising earlier each night.

flow.parent: Expect about 1 minute-mark of movement in a week, the stars shifting against the clock by about 7 degrees (a minute-mark is 6 degrees). It is easy to be a mark out by eye, so the month total is more reliable than any one week. The pointer stars move anticlockwise round the Pole Star. It is a small shift, so measure carefully.

flow.do: Repeat the drawing at the same time on day 15 and on day 22. Each time, write the date and compare with the one before.
flow.say: Two more times. The line should keep moving in the same direction. Do you see a pattern? How many minute-marks after three weeks?
flow.kid: Draw the line on day 15 and day 22. Compare each with the last.
flow.parent: Expect the line to have moved back about 3 to 4 minute-marks after three weeks. If the sky is cloudy on the night, use Stellarium Web with the date set, to see where the line would be.

flow.do: On day 29, draw the last sky clock. Lay all five side by side. Measure how far the line moved from day 1 to day 29, in minute-marks. Each minute-mark is 6 degrees. Work out the degrees. Then ask how many hours of sky-turning that is.
flow.say: Count the minute-marks between the first line and the last. Multiply by 6 to get degrees. The sky turns 15 degrees an hour. How many hours of turning is that? So at the same clock time, the sky of next month looks like the sky of how many hours later?
flow.kid: Count how far the line moved. Each mark is 6 degrees. Work out the degrees.

check.q: The line moved back by 5 minute-marks in four weeks. Each minute-mark is 6 degrees. About how many hours of the sky's turning is that?
check.why: 5 marks of 6 degrees is 30 degrees. The sky turns 15 degrees an hour, so 30 degrees is 2 hours. So at the same clock time, the sky in a month looks like the sky 2 hours later, because the Earth has moved a month round the Sun. If you picked 5 hours, you may have counted the marks as hours.

flow.parent: From day 1 to day 29 is 28 days, so the line should have moved about 28 degrees, which is about 4 to 5 minute-marks. Being a mark out is fine. This is the sky turning 4 minutes earlier each day, which adds up to about 2 hours of turning in a month.

challenges.title: Measure the Unreachable: how far is a tree you cannot walk to?
challenges.problem: There is a tall tree, a water tank or a building across a road or a field that you cannot walk to. Find out how far away it is, using only a baseline you can measure, a sheet of paper and a ruler.
constraints: You may not walk to the thing, or measure straight to it with a tape.
You may measure one baseline on your side, between two spots 5 to 10 metres apart.
You must draw a scale drawing of the triangle on paper.
Check your answer at the end with a map measuring tool or by pacing the distance with a grown-up.
materials: a flat board or a hard book, and 2 sheets of paper (tape two sheets together if the drawing is long)
a ruler, a pencil and a drawing pin or a small piece of clay
a measuring tape or a long string with knots every metre
a shoe or a cone to mark each end of the baseline
a friend or a grown-up to stand at the other end; with one child and no helper, use a cone, shoe or tall stick as the marker at B
general: Measure a baseline of 10 metres between points A and B. Choose a scale that fits your paper: 1 centimetre for 1 metre if the thing is within about 25 metres, or 1 centimetre for 2 metres if it is farther. Draw the baseline on the paper. At each end, draw a line towards the thing, then see where the two lines meet.
Make the baseline long compared with the distance. A baseline of about one-third of the distance works well.
Take your measurement three times and use the middle one, because one try can be a fluke.
creative: Use two photos taken from the two ends, and see how far the thing shifts against the background, as the thumb did.
Use a longer baseline for a farther thing, as astronomers use the whole width of the Earth's orbit for a star.
Pick a thing whose real distance a grown-up can find on a map, and test how close you can get.
challenges.safety: Choose a thing across a field or a quiet space, never across a busy road, and do not step into the road to measure. A grown-up stays with the child. Keep the drawing pin pointing down into the board, and put it in the clay when you are not using it. Rest the board on a chair or stool, not on the ground, so nobody kneels in the way of others.
challenges.your_turn: Now choose your own far thing, make a plan, draw the scale triangle and work out the distance. Check it against a map or by pacing. How close were you? What would you change next time to get closer?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about measuring the distance to something you cannot reach. It uses triangles, as surveyors do, and as astronomers do with parallax.

setup.art: A child at one end of a baseline and a friend at the other, with a tall tree across a field and two dotted lines from the two people to the tree.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a baseline between two spots. Pick a far thing to measure.

setup.art: A board with a sheet of paper, a pin and a ruler, with a line drawn from the pin towards the tree and another towards the friend.
setup.caption: 2. At the first spot, aim the ruler at the tree and at your friend. Draw both lines.

setup.art: A scale drawing of a triangle on paper, with the baseline marked 10 centimetres and the two lines meeting at the tree, with the distance measured.
setup.caption: 3. At the second spot, draw the same. Where the lines cross is the tree.

flow.do: Read the problem. Choose a far thing and decide on a baseline. Sketch the plan. Ask your child to guess the distance first.
flow.say: Surveyors found the distance across India this way. In 1802 they started the great survey near Chennai by measuring one baseline of several kilometres, and building triangles from it. How far do you think the tree is?
flow.kid: Pick a far tree or tank. How far do you think it is? Guess.

ask.q: How could a triangle help you find a distance you cannot measure?
good: If I know one side and two angles, I can draw the triangle.
I can draw it small on paper and measure.
The two lines from the ends meet at the tree.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Measure the Unreachable challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Stand at A with the board flat. Fix a sheet of paper on it. Stick a pin at a point near the bottom, called a. Put the ruler against the pin. Turn the ruler to point at your friend at B, and draw a line. Turn it to point at the thing, and draw a second line.
flow.say: Hold the ruler against the pin. Aim it at your friend and draw the line. Now aim at the tree and draw the second line. The angle between the lines is the angle the triangle has at A.
flow.kid: Put the pin in the paper. Aim the ruler at your friend. Draw a line. Aim at the tree.
flow.parent: Mark the baseline length on the first line, at the scale chosen. At 1 centimetre to 1 metre, a 10 metre baseline is 10 centimetres, and the point is called b. Keep the board flat and level.

flow.do: Move to B. Rest the board on a stool, chair or low wall with the pin at b. Turn the board until the ruler along the line b to a points at A. Keep it there. Now aim the ruler from b at the thing, and draw the second line. Where the two lines cross is the thing.
flow.say: Now we do the same from the other end. Make sure the line b to a points back at the first spot. Then aim at the tree and draw. See where the lines cross. Measure from a to the crossing with your ruler.
flow.kid: Move to the other end. Point the line back to the first end. Aim at the tree.

check.q: On your scale drawing, 1 centimetre stands for 2 metres. The crossing point is 19 centimetres from a. How far is the tree from spot A?
check.why: Each centimetre stands for 2 metres, so 19 centimetres stands for 19 times 2, which is 38 metres. If you picked 19, you forgot to double. If you picked 9.5, you halved instead of doubling.

flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, give out jobs: one holds the board and aims, one stands at the far marker, one measures the baseline, one writes down. Swap and compare the three drawings; the middle answer is the one to trust.

flow.do: Check your answer. A grown-up measures the distance on a map or by pacing. Work out how many metres you were out and what fraction of the distance. Talk about what would make the answer better.
flow.say: How close were we? Out by a few metres is very good. What could we change next time? A longer baseline? More careful aiming?
flow.kid: How close were you? What would you change next time?

ask.q: What would give a more accurate answer next time?
good: A longer baseline.
Aiming the ruler more carefully.
Taking the measurement three times.

flow.parent: Any answer within 20 percent is a good result for the first attempt. If your answer was far out, check that the board did not turn between sights and that the baseline was measured straight.

worksheets.title: The Turning Sky and the Pole Star (core)

items.p: Why do the stars seem to cross the sky during a night?
opts: The Earth spins, so we turn past the stars
The stars all circle the Earth once a day
The Sun pushes the stars across the sky
The stars are on a dome that the Moon turns
items.why: The Earth spins once in about a day, and we spin with it. So the sky seems to turn the other way, like scenery seen from a train. Picking 'the stars circle the Earth' is the picture people held for thousands of years. The photos of star trails and the pendulum show that the Earth is what turns.

items.p: The sky turns about ____ degrees every hour.
items.why: A full turn is 360 degrees, and it takes about 24 hours. 360 divided by 24 is 15. So every hour the stars move through 15 degrees, about one and a half fists at arm's length.

items.p: The sky turns 15 degrees every hour. A half circle is 180 degrees. So the sky turns a half circle in ____ hours.
items.why: 180 divided by 15 is 12. So a star that rises in the east will be in the west about 12 hours later. A strong answer shows the division.

items.p: The Pole Star is the brightest star in the night sky.
items.why: False. The Pole Star is only about as bright as the stars of the Saptarishi. Many stars look brighter, including Sirius. The Pole Star is special because of where it is, almost exactly in line with the Earth's axis, and not because of how bright it is.

items.p: Which two stars of the Saptarishi point towards the Pole Star?
opts: The two stars at the outer edge of the bowl, Kratu and Pulaha
The two stars at the end of the handle
The two middle stars of the handle
The brightest and the faintest star
items.why: Draw a line through the two stars on the outer edge of the bowl, the ones furthest from the handle. Carry the line on about five times the gap between them, and it meets the Pole Star. The handle stars point to other things, such as the bright star Arcturus.

items.p: All the other stars circle the Pole Star. Why does the Pole Star itself hardly move?
items.a: The Earth's axis points almost straight at the Pole Star. As the Earth spins round its axis, the star stays in the same place in the sky, just as the tip of a spinning top's axis stays still while everything else goes round.
items.why: A strong answer links the star to the axis. The Pole Star is not special in itself. It looks still because it lies along the line the Earth spins round.

items.p: Match each place to about how high the Pole Star stands above the northern horizon.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The Pole Star's height is the same as the latitude of the place. The further north, the higher the star. A strong answer notices the pattern in the numbers.

items.p: A traveller walks north, from Chennai towards Delhi. What happens to the Pole Star's height above the horizon?
opts: It slowly rises higher
It slowly sinks lower
It stays the same
It moves to the south
items.why: The Pole Star's height equals the latitude, and latitude grows as you go north. So the star climbs. Picking 'stays the same' is a natural idea, because the star never seems to move. It moves only when the traveller does.

items.p: Label this drawing of a ball for the Earth: the Earth's axis, the direction to the Pole Star, the observer's flat horizon, and the angle that equals the latitude.
items.a: The axis runs through the ball from pole to pole. The direction to the Pole Star runs parallel to the axis. The horizon is a flat line touching the ball at the observer. The angle between the horizon and the line to the Pole Star is the latitude.
items.why: Because the Pole Star is so far away, the direction to it is parallel to the axis from anywhere on the Earth. The angle between that direction and the flat ground is the latitude.
items.art: A ball with a vertical line through it, a dotted line to a star above, a small observer on the ball with a flat card as horizon, and four empty label lines.

items.p: At midnight, we see the same stars in every month of the year.
items.why: False. A star rises about 4 minutes earlier each night, so the sky shifts by about 2 hours each month. The group of stars highest at midnight changes through the year, because the Earth is moving round the Sun.

items.p: A star rises at 9 pm tonight. About what time will it rise one month from now?
opts: About 7 pm
About 9 pm
About 11 pm
About 3 pm
items.why: A star rises about 4 minutes earlier each day, so after 30 days it rises about 2 hours earlier. 9 pm take away 2 hours is 7 pm. Picking 11 pm goes the wrong way. Picking 9 pm forgets that the Earth has moved.

items.p: Sort these groups of stars into the ones best seen on winter evenings and the ones best seen on summer and monsoon evenings.
items.a: see items
items.why: The groups opposite the Sun at midnight in winter are Taurus, Gemini and Orion. In summer, the groups opposite the Sun are Scorpius, Sagittarius and the stars near them. A strong answer says why the two sets are on opposite sides of the sky.

items.p: You hold a pencil at arm's length and swap eyes. Then you bring the pencil to half that distance and swap eyes again. What do you see?
opts: The jump against the wall is about twice as big
The jump is the same
The jump is much smaller
The pencil does not jump at all
items.why: The nearer a thing is, the more the two eyes disagree about where it is. At half the distance, the jump is about twice as big. Picking 'the same' means forgetting that near things change more than far things.

items.p: You cannot see a star's parallax by closing one eye and then the other, but astronomers can measure it. What do they do differently?
items.a: The stars are so far away that the gap between two eyes gives a shift far too small to see. Astronomers look at the star six months apart, from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit, so the baseline is about 300 million kilometres. The shift is then big enough to measure with a telescope.
items.why: A strong answer says that a longer baseline gives a bigger shift. The jump of the thumb gets bigger when the baseline is longer.

items.p: Two friends in Pune, Kavitha and Rohan, talk about whether the Earth moves round the Sun.

views.says: If the Earth moved round the Sun, the nearby stars would seem to shift against the far ones during the year. Nobody sees a shift, so the Earth must be still.
The stars are so far away that the shift is far too small to see with our eyes. That is why we see no shift, even though the Earth moves.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say what the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks Rohan and gives the evidence: in 1838 Bessel measured the tiny shift of a star with a very precise instrument. It also gives Kavitha her due: her argument is sound, because if stars were near, there would be a shift. She did not know how far away they were.
items.why: Kavitha's argument is the one that Tycho Brahe made. It is a good argument with a missing fact. Better instruments later found the fact.

items.p: Draw the stars as you would see them looking north for one hour. Show the Pole Star and three stars at different distances from it, with arcs showing how they move.
items.a: The Pole Star stays at the middle. Each of the three other stars draws an arc round it, anticlockwise, all of the same angle, 15 degrees. Stars further from the Pole Star draw longer arcs.
items.why: Every star turns through the same angle in the same time. Stars far from the Pole Star travel along bigger circles, so their arcs are longer, but the angle is the same.
items.art: A page with a small dot in the middle labelled Pole Star, and three smaller dots at different distances from it, with room to draw arcs.

items.p: Canopus gives out about 400 times as much light as Sirius, yet Sirius looks brighter in the sky. What does this tell you?
opts: Sirius must be much nearer to us than Canopus
Sirius must be hotter than Canopus
Canopus must be moving away
The sky is darker near Sirius
items.why: How bright a star looks depends on how much light it gives out and how far away it is. Canopus is truly far more powerful, but it is about 310 light-years away. Sirius is only about 8.6 light-years away, so it looks brighter.

items.p: To work out how much light a star really gives out, you must first know its ____.
items.why: A star looks fainter the farther away it is. So you cannot tell how powerful it is from how bright it looks, until you know how far away it is. This is why parallax matters.

items.p: Henrietta Leavitt's discovery about pulsing stars helped astronomers measure distances too great for parallax.
items.why: True. In 1912 she found that Cepheid stars that pulse more slowly are truly brighter. If you know a Cepheid's true brightness and see how bright it looks, you can work out its distance. A strong answer says that this method reaches far beyond parallax.

items.p: Three stars look red, yellow and blue-white. Which has the hottest surface?
opts: The blue-white star
The red star
The yellow star
They are all equally hot
items.why: The hotter a star's surface, the bluer its light. A red star is cooler, a yellow star is in the middle, and a blue-white star is hottest. A piece of iron glows red first, then yellow, then white, as it gets hotter.

items.p: Match each star to its colour and its surface temperature.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Colour is a thermometer for stars. A strong answer says why the order of the colours matches the order of the temperatures.

items.p: Betelgeuse is red and huge. A friend says red stars must be the hottest, because red is the colour of fire. What would you say?
items.a: In a star, red means cooler. Blue-white stars like Rigel are much hotter. A glowing piece of iron is red at first and turns yellow and then white-blue as it gets hotter. Betelgeuse is cool for a star, but it is so big that it still gives out a great deal of light.
items.why: A strong answer separates temperature from size. A cool star can be huge and bright. The colour only tells the temperature of the surface.

items.p: Two bright dots are in the evening sky. One flickers and flashes different colours. The other shines steadily. Which is more likely to be a planet?
opts: The steady one
The flickering one
Both are planets
Neither can be a planet
items.why: A planet is a tiny disc, so the wobble of the air averages out and its light looks steady. A star is a point, so the air flickers all of it at once. If you picked the flickering one, think of the foil with the tiny hole.

items.p: A star low near the horizon twinkles more than the same star when it is overhead.
items.why: True. Low in the sky, a star's light crosses much more air before it reaches your eye, so there is more bending and flickering. Overhead, it passes through the thinnest layer of air.

items.p: Why do planets twinkle much less than stars?
items.a: A star is a single point of light, so moving air bends all of it at once and it flickers. A planet is a tiny disc made of many points, and the flickers of the different points cancel out, so its light is steadier.
items.why: A strong answer says that the difference is in the shape of the light, a point or a tiny disc, and not in the object being near or far.

items.p: Put these cities in order of how high the Pole Star stands, from the lowest to the highest: Delhi, Kanyakumari, Mumbai, Chennai.
items.why: The Pole Star's height equals the latitude. Kanyakumari is about 8 degrees, Chennai about 13, Mumbai about 19 and Delhi about 29.

items.p: You stand on the equator. Which stars never set for you?
opts: None, every star rises and sets
The stars near the Pole Star
The stars of the Saptarishi
The brightest stars
items.why: On the equator, the Pole Star is on the horizon, and every star circles in a path that goes below it. So every star rises and sets. In Delhi, stars near the Pole Star never set. Picking the Saptarishi forgets that the Pole Star is on the horizon.

items.p: A star rises about ____ hours earlier each month.
items.why: A star rises about 4 minutes earlier each day. In 30 days that is 120 minutes, which is 2 hours.

items.p: Label this drawing of the Earth's orbit: the Sun, the Earth in January, the group of stars highest at midnight, and the group hidden by the Sun's glare.
items.a: The Sun in the middle. The Earth on the ring. The midnight group on the side of the Earth away from the Sun. The hidden group on the far side of the Sun from the Earth.
items.why: At midnight we look away from the Sun, so the group highest then is opposite the Sun. The group behind the Sun is up in the daytime and hidden by sunlight.
items.art: The Sun at the middle of a ring with the Earth on it, groups of stars drawn round the outside, and four empty label lines.

items.p: In the thumb test, one thing jumped 30 centimetres against the wall and another jumped 15 centimetres. What can you say?
opts: The second thing is about twice as far away as the first
The second thing is nearer than the first
Both are the same distance away
The second thing is half as big
items.why: A smaller jump means a farther thing. Half the jump means about twice the distance. Picking 'nearer' reverses the rule. The size of a thing does not change its jump.

items.p: Two scholars talk about how the first settlers found tiny islands in the Pacific.

views.says: Most early voyages were accidents. Canoes were blown off course, and those that reached islands were lucky.

views.who: David Lewis and the crew of Hokulea, 1970s
views.says: People crossed on purpose. In 1976 a navigator took Hokulea from Hawaii to Tahiti using only stars, swells and birds.

items.ask: Which scholar do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say what the other gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence. The 1976 voyage shows that purposeful navigation is possible, which supports Lewis. Sharp may be right that some voyages were accidents, and the 1976 voyage does not prove what happened thousands of years ago.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. Both answers use evidence, and a modern voyage shows what is possible, but not what really happened.

items.p: Draw the Earth with its axis, the direction to the Pole Star, and a person in Chennai with a flat horizon. Mark the angle between the horizon and the Pole Star, and write its size.
items.a: A ball with a line through it from pole to pole. A line from Chennai parallel to the axis towards the Pole Star. A flat horizon at Chennai. An angle of 13 degrees between the horizon and the line.
items.why: The angle equals the latitude, 13 degrees for Chennai. A strong drawing makes the line to the star parallel to the axis.
items.art: A circle for the Earth with a vertical axis line, a star at the top, and a dot at a low-middle position for Chennai with room to draw a horizon.

items.p: Explain why a longer baseline gives a bigger parallax shift. Use the pencil and your two eyes as an example.
items.a: If your eyes were further apart, the pencil would look more different from each one, so it would jump more against the wall. The same is true for a star. Looking from the two ends of the Earth's orbit, which is far wider than the gap between eyes, makes the star's shift big enough to measure.
items.why: A strong answer connects baseline to the size of the shift. The two eyes and the Earth's orbit are the same idea at different sizes.

items.p: Three people in a town talk about whether to turn off some street lights at night.

views.says: Bright lights hide the stars. A child who never sees the Milky Way never wonders about it. We should switch off lights we do not need.
Lights make the street safe for people walking home. I would not want to lose them.
Many insects and birds are confused by bright lights at night. Switching them off helps wildlife too.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Use what you know about stars and light. Then say what one of the others gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and gives a reason from the unit, for example that light pollution hides faint stars, so Revathi's point is true. It also gives credit to another view. Farhan is right that lights help safety, and a good plan might use shielded lights that point down.
items.why: All three have good points, and the best solution tries to meet more than one need. Shields that stop light from going up help stargazers and wildlife, and still light the street.

items.p: The Pole Star is about 0.7 degrees away from the exact north pole of the sky. What does this do to the rule that its height equals your latitude?
opts: The rule is right to within about a degree
The rule is completely wrong
The rule works only in Delhi
The rule works only at the equator
items.why: Because the star is a fraction of a degree from the pole, it makes a small circle round the pole each day, and its height changes by up to about 0.7 degrees. For measuring with a straw and a protractor, that is far less than the error of the tool. So the rule is useful to about a degree.

items.p: A sailor sees that the Pole Star is 13 degrees high. What does this tell the sailor, and what does it not tell?
items.a: It tells the sailor how far north they are, about 13 degrees north. It does not tell how far east or west they are. For that, the sailor needs to compare the time on the ship with the time at a known place.
items.why: A strong answer sees that one star gives only one number, the latitude. The height of the Pole Star is the same along the whole line of latitude.

items.p: Two stars give out exactly the same amount of light. One is twice as far away as the other. How bright does the farther one look compared with the nearer one?
opts: One quarter as bright
Half as bright
The same
Twice as bright
items.why: Light spreads out as it travels, so twice as far means the same light covers four times the area. Each part gets a quarter. Picking 'half' forgets that the spreading happens in two directions.

items.p: If the Earth stopped spinning, the stars would stop seeming to circle the Pole Star.
items.why: True. The turning of the sky is caused by the spin of the Earth. If the spin stopped, the stars would hang still in the sky. The only slow shift left would be the one caused by the Earth's journey round the Sun.

items.p: Four thousand seven hundred years ago, a star called Thuban was the pole star. Today it is Polaris. Explain why the pole star changes.
items.a: The Earth's axis slowly wobbles, like a spinning top, and traces a circle in the sky once in about 26,000 years. So the axis points at different stars over time. Thuban was near the pole then, Polaris is now, and in about 12,000 years it will be Vega.
items.why: A strong answer names the wobble and the very long time it takes. The change is so slow that nobody sees it in a lifetime.

items.p: In about 12,000 years, a different star will be near the north celestial pole. What is the best reason?
opts: The Earth's axis slowly wobbles and points at different stars
The stars all move towards the pole
The Pole Star will burn out
The Earth will stop spinning
items.why: The Earth's axis traces a slow circle in the sky because of a wobble called precession. It makes a complete circle in about 26,000 years. Picking 'the stars move towards the pole' is wrong, because stars move only very slowly.

items.p: Sort these into the ones where parallax can be used and the ones where it is too small to use.
cats: Parallax is too small to use
items: A pencil at arm's length, with two eyes
A tree across a road, using a baseline of 10 metres
A nearby star, using the Earth's orbit as the baseline
A star in a distant galaxy, using the Earth's orbit
Parallax is too small to use
A mountain 100 kilometres away, with two eyes
Parallax is too small to use
items.a: see items
items.why: Parallax works when the baseline is big enough compared with the distance. For far things, astronomers need other methods, such as Cepheids.

items.p: What are stars made of, mostly?
opts: Hydrogen and helium
Iron and rock
Oxygen and nitrogen
Carbon and water
items.why: Cecilia Payne showed in 1925 that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Most people at the time believed stars were made of the same stuff as the Earth. Iron and rock are rare in stars.

items.p: Draw the sky as seen by someone standing exactly at the North Pole. Show where the Pole Star is, and how the other stars move.
items.a: The Pole Star is straight overhead. The other stars circle round it in flat circles, parallel to the ground, and none rises or sets.
items.why: At the North Pole the Earth's axis points straight up, so the Pole Star is overhead, and every star goes round it at a constant height. The stars never rise or set.
items.art: A person at the middle of a large circle that stands for the horizon, with a star directly overhead and room to draw circles.

items.p: At the equator, no star is circumpolar. Explain why.
items.a: At the equator, the Pole Star sits on the horizon. A star can only be circumpolar if its circle round the Pole Star stays above the horizon, and with the Pole Star at 0 degrees there is no room for a circle above it. So every star rises and sets.
items.why: A strong answer uses the rule that stars within your latitude's number of degrees of the pole are circumpolar. At 0 degrees, that is none.

items.p: From Kanyakumari, at about 8 degrees north, a person can see the Southern Cross low in the south on spring evenings.
items.why: True. At 8 degrees north, stars within about 8 degrees of the south pole never rise, but the Southern Cross is much farther from the south pole than that, and rises and sets. It is low in the sky because it is far to the south. From Kashmir it cannot be seen.

items.p: A visitor says: 'The stars are twinkling, so they must be giving out light unevenly.' What is the best reply?
opts: The flicker is made by the Earth's moving air, and stars seen from space do not twinkle
You are right, stars flicker like candles
The stars are being pulled by the Moon
Stars twinkle because they are close
items.why: Twinkling happens in the air above us, where patches of different temperature bend the light. Photographs taken from space telescopes show steady stars. The visitor's idea is natural, because it looks as if the star itself flickers.

items.p: The thumb test and the Gaia spacecraft both measure parallax. Say one thing that is the same about them and one thing that is different.
items.a: Both look at the same thing from two places and measure how much it seems to shift. The baseline is different: for the thumb it is the gap between the eyes, a few centimetres, and for Gaia it is the width of the Earth's orbit, hundreds of millions of kilometres, so Gaia can measure stars.
items.why: A strong answer sees one method at two scales.

items.p: Draw the Sun, the Earth's orbit, and the Earth at two points six months apart. Show a near star shifting against faraway stars as seen from the two points.
items.a: The Sun at the middle of an oval ring. The Earth on opposite sides of the ring. A near star with lines to the Earth at each point, and the two lines ending at different spots among the faraway stars.
items.why: The Earth's orbit is the baseline. From opposite sides, the near star appears in slightly different places against the far stars. The size of that shift tells the distance.
items.art: A Sun at the middle of an oval orbit with two empty Earth positions marked, a near star on one side and a row of small faraway stars on the other.

quiz.p: A photograph of the northern sky is taken with the camera open for one hour. Each star leaves an arc. What part of a full circle is each arc?
opts: One twenty-fourth of a full circle
A quarter of a full circle
A whole circle
One sixtieth of a full circle
quiz.why: The sky turns once in about 24 hours, so in one hour it turns one twenty-fourth of a circle, which is 15 degrees. Picking a quarter would be the arc after six hours.

quiz.p: What is special about the position of the Pole Star?
opts: The Earth's axis points almost straight at it
It is the nearest star to the Earth
It is the star that the Sun passes in front of
It is exactly overhead everywhere in India
quiz.why: The Pole Star lies almost exactly along the line the Earth spins round. That is why it seems to stay still while the others turn. It is not near, and it is not overhead in India. In Chennai it is only about a fist above the northern horizon.

quiz.p: A traveller sees the Pole Star 20 degrees above the northern horizon. About what is her latitude?
opts: About 20 degrees north
About 70 degrees north
About 20 degrees south
About 90 degrees north
quiz.why: The Pole Star's height equals the latitude, so 20 degrees high means about 20 degrees north. Picking 70 gives the angle measured down from straight overhead instead. At 90 degrees north, you stand at the pole.

opts: A star that circles the Pole Star without ever dipping below your horizon
A star that circles the Sun
A star that is exactly at the pole
A star that is seen in every country
quiz.why: A circumpolar star goes round the Pole Star in a circle that stays above the horizon, so it never sets. Which stars are circumpolar depends on your latitude, and so a star can be circumpolar in Delhi and not in Chennai.

quiz.p: Why can Orion not be seen at night in June?
opts: The Sun is near Orion in the sky, so it is up in the day and hidden by sunlight
Orion moves to the other side of the Earth
Orion is switched off in summer
The Moon covers Orion
quiz.why: In June, the Earth is on the side of its orbit where the Sun lies in the direction of Orion. At night we look away from the Sun, so we look at other stars. Orion is up in the day, but daylight hides it.

quiz.p: How much earlier does a star rise each night?
opts: About 4 minutes
About 1 hour
About 15 minutes
The same time every night
quiz.why: The Earth moves about one degree round the Sun each day, so we have to turn about a degree further to face a star. That takes about 4 minutes. Over a year, the 4 minutes add up to a whole day.

quiz.p: A thing seems to jump a long way against the background when you swap eyes. What does this tell you?
opts: The thing is close to you
The thing is very far from you
The thing is moving
The thing is very big
quiz.why: The nearer a thing is, the more the two eyes disagree about where it is, and the bigger the jump. A far thing barely jumps. This is how distance is measured from parallax.

quiz.p: Why do astronomers use the Earth's orbit as the baseline for measuring the distance to a star?
opts: Stars are so far away that only a very long baseline gives a shift big enough to measure
The Earth's orbit is a perfect circle
Astronomers cannot use their eyes
The Sun's light helps to measure it
quiz.why: The shift of a star is the tiny angle made by a baseline, so the longer the baseline, the bigger the shift. The Earth's orbit is about 300 million kilometres wide, and it is the longest baseline astronomers can use without leaving the solar system.

quiz.p: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, but there are stars far more powerful than it. Why does Sirius look so bright?
opts: It is very near, only about 8.6 light-years away, and it is also quite powerful
It is the hottest star in the sky
It is the largest star in the sky
It is moving towards us fast
quiz.why: How bright a star looks depends on both its distance and its true brightness. Sirius gives out about 25 times as much light as the Sun, and it is very near. Stars like Rigel are much more powerful, but they are far away.

quiz.p: Which colour of star is the hottest?
opts: Blue-white
Red
Yellow
Orange
quiz.why: The hotter a star, the bluer its light. Red is the coolest of these, then orange, yellow and finally blue-white. Fire is a hint: iron glows red, then yellow, then white as it heats up.

quiz.p: Why do stars twinkle while planets usually shine steadily?
opts: A star is a point of light that the moving air bends all at once, and a planet is a tiny disc whose flickers average out
Stars are hotter than planets
Planets make their own steady light
Stars are closer than planets
quiz.why: The air bends the light of a star as a single point, so it seems to flicker. A planet's light comes from a tiny disc, and the flickers cancel out. Planets do not make light, and stars are farther than planets.

quiz.p: How can you tell that a bright dot is a planet by watching it for several weeks?
opts: It slowly moves against the pattern of stars
It twinkles more every week
It gets redder every week
It gets closer to the Pole Star
quiz.why: Planets are wanderers. They shift slowly against the fixed pattern of the stars over days and weeks, because they go round the Sun. Stars keep their places. A planet does not get redder or move towards the Pole Star.

applications: Finding latitude from the height of the Pole Star, as sailors and travellers did for centuries before satellites.
Measuring distances to stars by parallax, which is the first step in measuring the size of the universe.
Measuring distances far beyond parallax using Cepheid stars, following the work of Henrietta Leavitt.
Surveying a country or a field by triangles, as the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India began to do in 1802.
Pointing a telescope at a star, which has to follow the sky's steady turn of 15 degrees an hour.
Keeping calendars and festival dates, such as Makar Sankranti, in step with the Sun's place among the stars.
Finding a ship's or a plane's place by satellites, which use the same geometry as triangles and parallax.
Judging distance with two eyes, as a cat does before a jump or a cricketer does before catching a high ball.
Designing dark-sky parks and shielded street lights, so people can still see the stars from a town.
Sorting stars by colour into types to learn their temperature, a method started by Annie Jump Cannon and her colleagues.

open_questions.q: How far away is the Pole Star, exactly?
open_questions.why_open: Different measurements have given between about 320 and 450 light-years. Polaris is a pulsing star, and is too bright for some instruments, so astronomers are still working on a good answer.

open_questions.q: How did the first people find tiny islands across the open Pacific?
open_questions.why_open: A modern voyage shows it can be done by stars, swells and birds. No one can prove how it was done thousands of years ago.

open_questions.q: Did Ice Age people already map the stars?
open_questions.why_open: Some scholars think the dots in the cave paintings of Lascaux show the Pleiades. Others see only random dots, and there is no way to check what the painters meant.

open_questions.q: Are there faint stars very near the Sun that we have not found yet?
open_questions.why_open: A very faint, cool star-like object was announced only in 2014, about 7 light-years away. There may be more such dim neighbours that we cannot see.

open_questions.q: What will our descendants call the stars of the Saptarishi in 100,000 years?
open_questions.why_open: The stars slowly drift, and the ladle will bend out of shape. No one knows whether the names will last.

open_questions.q: Why is it that nearly all the stars we see are in our own galaxy?
open_questions.why_open: Almost every star you can see by eye is within a few thousand light-years. Why we live in a spot with so many bright stars nearby is not something astronomers have a settled answer for.

maths.problem: The sky turns 15 degrees every hour. How many degrees does it turn in 6 hours? What fraction of a full circle is that?
maths.answer: 90 degrees, which is a quarter of a full circle.
maths.explain: 15 times 6 is 90. A full circle is 360 degrees, and 90 is one quarter of 360, because 4 times 90 is 360.
maths.context: This is about the Turning Sky experiment, where you measured how far a star moves in an hour.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the angle for one hour by the number of hours tells you where a star will be later, which is how the sky clock works.

maths.problem: A fist covers about 10 degrees. In the Turning Sky test, a star went from 3 fists to 1 and a half fists above a roof edge in one hour. How many degrees did it move? How many hours would a full circle of 360 degrees take at that rate?
maths.answer: 15 degrees. A full circle takes 24 hours.
maths.explain: The star moved 3 take away 1.5, which is 1.5 fists. 1.5 times 10 is 15 degrees. 360 divided by 15 is 24. So the full turn takes 24 hours, which is one day.
maths.context: This is about the fist measurements in the Turning Sky experiment.
maths.why_maths: Working with fists and degrees turns a rough measurement into the rate at which the Earth spins.

maths.problem: Kanyakumari is at 8 degrees north and Delhi is at 29 degrees north. By how many degrees does the Pole Star climb on a journey from one to the other? One degree of latitude is about 111 kilometres. About how far north of Kanyakumari is Delhi?
maths.explain: 29 take away 8 is 21 degrees. 21 times 111 is 2,331, which is about 2,300 kilometres. So the Pole Star climbs one degree for about every 111 kilometres you go north.
maths.context: This is about how the Pole Star's height depends on how far north you are.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying turns a change in the star's height into a distance travelled, so a star can work as a map.

maths.problem: In the Jump of Your Thumb test, a pencil at 25 centimetres jumped 60 centimetres, at 50 centimetres it jumped 28, and at 100 centimetres it jumped 11. Multiply the distance by the jump for each. What do you notice?
maths.answer: About 1,500, 1,400 and 1,100. The three answers are fairly close to each other.
maths.explain: 25 times 60 is 1,500. 50 times 28 is 1,400. 100 times 11 is 1,100. They are not exactly equal, but they are of a similar size. If the jump halves each time the distance doubles, the answer stays about the same. It drops a little because the wall is only 3 metres away.
maths.context: This is about the results of the Jump of Your Thumb experiment.
maths.why_maths: Spotting that distance times jump stays roughly the same helps you to use a jump to find an unknown distance.

maths.problem: A star rises 4 minutes earlier each day. How much earlier does it rise after 30 days? Give your answer in minutes and in hours.
maths.explain: 4 times 30 is 120 minutes. 120 divided by 60 is 2 hours. So after a month, a star rises 2 hours earlier.
maths.context: This is about why the stars at night change with the seasons.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small daily change by the days in a month shows how the evening sky shifts.

maths.problem: Sirius is 8.6 light-years away. One light-year is about 9.5 trillion kilometres. About how many trillion kilometres away is Sirius?
maths.explain: 8.6 times 9.5 is about 82, because 8 times 9.5 is 76 and 0.6 times 9.5 is 5.7, which makes 81.7. So Sirius is about 82 trillion kilometres away.
maths.context: This is about the distance of Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.
maths.why_maths: A light-year is a huge unit. Multiplying shows how large the number is in kilometres.

maths.problem: A star looks one quarter as bright when it is twice as far away. How bright does it look at 3 times the distance? At 10 times the distance?
maths.answer: One ninth as bright at 3 times the distance. One hundredth as bright at 10 times the distance.
maths.explain: The light spreads out over an area that grows as the distance times itself. 3 times 3 is 9, so one ninth. 10 times 10 is 100, so one hundredth.
maths.context: This is about why the brightness of a star depends on its distance.
maths.why_maths: Squaring the distance tells you how much fainter a star looks, which is needed to find its true brightness.

maths.problem: The Earth's axis traces a full circle of 360 degrees in the sky in about 26,000 years. About how many years does it take to move 1 degree?
maths.explain: 26,000 divided by 360 is about 72, because 72 times 360 is 25,920. So the pole moves 1 degree in about 72 years. This is also why Makar Sankranti slips by about one day every 72 years.
maths.context: This is about the slow wobble of the Earth's axis, which changes the Pole Star over thousands of years.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a huge time by a full circle gives a rate you can picture, and links two different facts about the sky.

how_we_found_out.story: For about 2,000 years, careful thinkers said that the Earth could not be moving. Their reason was a good one. If the Earth went round the Sun, they said, the nearer stars should seem to shift against the farther ones during the year, just as your thumb jumps when you swap eyes. Nobody could see any shift. In the 1500s the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe, who measured the stars more exactly than anyone before the telescope, used this as strong evidence that the Earth stands still. The followers of Copernicus replied that the stars must be too far away for the shift to show. It sounded like an excuse. Then in 1838 a German astronomer, Friedrich Bessel, watched a faint star called 61 Cygni for more than a year with a very precise instrument. He found a shift smaller than the width of a coin seen from about 16 kilometres away. It showed that the Earth moves, and that the star was about 11 light-years away.
how_we_found_out.who: Friedrich Bessel, a German astronomer, answering an argument made by Tycho Brahe
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: If the Earth moved, the nearer stars would seem to shift during the year. No shift had been seen, so the Earth must stand still. The stars are in fact far more distant than anyone had guessed, so the shift is too small to see by eye, and was found only in 1838.

playtest: Walked through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Jump of Your Thumb needs a bare wall and 3 metres of floor. With a 1.5 metre wall strip and the child standing on a marked spot, the pencil's jump comes out near 60, 28 and 11 centimetres for 25, 50 and 100 centimetres, but eyes differ, so the step tells the parent to look for the pattern rather than the numbers. It is the one real investigation in the spine and works indoors by day. Ball, Straw and Far Star works with any ball and a star on the wall, but the angles are hard to read exactly, so the step says that numbers may be 5 degrees out and asks for the pattern. The Turning Sky, the Pole Star Height and the Dhruva's Clock diary need a clear evening sky with a view to the east or west, or to the north, and they are not in the spine. In the south of India the Pole Star is low and can be hidden by haze or buildings, so the steps give Stellarium Web as the fallback. The Twinkle and Colour activity uses a hot tawa and a flame, so a grown-up does all the heating and the child sits back. The Year in a Room cards give the star group highest at midnight in each month, which is correct to about a month because the groups are large. Facts a reader should check before publishing: the exact distances of Polaris, the 1976 Hokule'a details, the words of the Udana, Rig Veda and Tirukkural lines, the claim about Lascaux, and the dates of the Great Trigonometrical Survey. The spine is the intro, the thumb experiment, the ball and straw model, the explanations, roots and the quiz, about 95 minutes over two sessions.
